title: The 10% trick
concept: 10% is the foundation of all tip math. Moving the decimal one place left gives you 10% of any number instantly. From there you can build any tip in seconds.
shortcut: 10% of $65 = $6.50 (just move the decimal). Double it for 20% = $13.00. Add half for 15% = $9.75. Master this one move and every tip becomes a two-second calculation.
realWorldHint: Use this at every restaurant, bar, and salon for the rest of your life.

title: Tipping shortcuts — 15%, 18%, 20%
concept: Every tip percentage builds on 10%. Once you can find 10% instantly (move the decimal left), 20% is double, 15% is 10% plus half, and 18% is 10% + 5% + a small 3% bump. The bigger your bill, the better the $X-per-$100 rule works.
shortcut: Per $100 in bill: 20% = $20, 18% = $18, 15% = $15. For $240, multiply by 2.4. For odd amounts, find 10% first, then build from there. 18% = 10% + 5% + 3%. 20% = double 10%. 15% = 10% + half of 10%.
realWorldHint: Pull this out the next time the check lands and you're second-guessing the tip.

title: Split any check in your head
concept: Bill splitting isn't a math problem — it's a social moment. Be the person at the table who solves the check in five seconds, while everyone else is still squinting at calculators. The trick: tip the full bill first, then divide. Splitting then tipping shortchanges the server and confuses everyone.
shortcut: Always: Total → add tip → divide by people. A $80 bill, 20% tip = $96, split 4 ways = $24 each. For odd numbers (3 or 5 people), round the per-person share up a dollar — covers the math and the awkward.
example:
Bill: $80.00
20% tip = $16.00
Total = $96.00
Per person (÷ 4) = $24.00

Odd split:
$120 bill, 20% tip = $144
÷ 3 = $48 each
realWorldHint: Use this when the group check arrives and everyone's reaching for their phone.

title: The real cost of 'free' deals
concept: 'Free' is rarely free. Buy 2 Get 1 Free is 33% off, not 50%. Buy 1 Get 1 Half Off is 25% off, not 50%. 'Buy 3 for $10' is just a unit-price calculation in disguise. The math the store hopes you skip: per-item cost = total paid ÷ items received.
shortcut: Per-item cost = total paid ÷ items received. B2G1 free: pay 2, get 3, per-item = (2 × price) ÷ 3. B1G1 half off: pay 1.5, get 2, per-item = 0.75 × price. Always ask: do I actually need all of them?
example:
Shampoo $9 each, B2G1 free:
Pay $18 for 3
Per bottle = $6
Real discount = 33%

B1G1 50% off $20:
Pay $30 for 2
Per item = $15
Real discount = 25%
realWorldHint: Run this before you grab a 'buy one get one' deal you didn't come in for.

title: Stacking discounts
concept: Two discounts stacked don't add up. 20% off plus 10% off isn't 30% off — the second discount applies to the already-reduced price. You always save a little less than the sum suggests. Before you stack, know the singles: 10% = move decimal, 25% = divide by 4, 50% = halve it.
shortcut: Apply discounts one at a time. $100 → 20% off → $80 → 10% off → $72. Saving: $28, not $30. Quick rule: each 10% combo loses about 1% to stacking. Two 50%-off coupons would only be 75% off, not 100%.
realWorldHint: Use this at checkout when a coupon stacks on top of a sale price.

title: Coupon vs cashback — which saves more?
concept: A 20% coupon and 5% cashback aren't the same. The coupon applies to the sticker price. The cashback applies to what you actually pay after the coupon. They stack, but the order matters — coupon first, cashback second, on the smaller amount.
shortcut: Coupon saves: price × coupon%. Cashback saves: (price after coupon) × cashback%. Bigger % almost always wins outright. For stacked deals: do coupon first, cashback on the remainder.
example:
Item $100:
20% coupon = $80 paid
5% cashback on $80 = $4 back
Net cost = $76

Vs no coupon:
5% cashback on $100 = $5
Net cost = $95
Coupon wins by $19
realWorldHint: Pull this up when you're choosing between a coupon code and a cashback offer.

title: What you actually pay: discount + tax
concept: You see '30% off' but you still pay sales tax on the sale price. The checkout total isn't the sticker price. Sale price × (1 + tax%) = real total. Most people forget the tax or apply it to the original price.
shortcut: Discount first, tax second. Never the other way. Sale price = original × (1 − discount%). Final = sale × (1 + tax%). Quick: knock off the discount, add ~10% for tax, check your budget.
example:
$80 shirt, 30% off, 9% tax:
Sale price = $80 × 0.70 = $56
With tax = $56 × 1.09 = $61.04

Forgot the tax? You'd budget $56 and be short $5.
realWorldHint: Use this at the register so the final price never surprises you.

title: Is Uber One / Costco / DashPass worth it?
concept: Membership programs charge a fee for per-use savings. Below break-even, the membership loses money. Above break-even, every additional use is pure savings. The math: break-even uses = fee ÷ saving per use.
shortcut: Break-even uses = fee ÷ per-use saving (round up). If you'll use it more than that in the same period, it pays for itself. DashPass $10/mo saving $3/order → 4 orders/mo breaks even. Order 8/mo → save $14/mo.
example:
DashPass: $10/month, save $3/delivery
Break-even = $10 ÷ $3 = 4 deliveries/mo

Costco: $65/year, save $8/visit
Break-even = $65 ÷ $8 = 9 visits/yr

Uber One: $10/mo, save $2/ride
Break-even = 5 rides/mo
realWorldHint: Run this before you renew Costco, Prime, or a delivery membership.

title: How retailers manipulate value
concept: Most pricing you see in stores is theater. Anchoring (crossed-out 'original' prices), decoy pricing (the medium size designed to make the large look like a deal), charm pricing ($9.99 vs $10), MSRP fiction, and inflated 'regular' prices during BOGO promos are all designed to bypass your math brain.
shortcut: Always ask: would I pay this price WITHOUT the 'discount' framing? If the 'original' price is unfamiliar or unverifiable, ignore it. Compare to competitor pricing, not to the store's anchor.
example:
Movie theater popcorn:
Small $4 · Medium $7 · Large $7.50
The medium is the 'decoy' — it makes the large look like a steal. Without it, you'd compare $4 vs $7.50 differently.

BOGO grocery scam (2024 lawsuit):
Chicken wings normally $11.99
During BOGO: 'regular' price = $19.99
Real cost: ~$9.99/lb either way
realWorldHint: Keep this in mind every time a store flashes a 'limited time' price.

title: Your real subscription bill
concept: Most people have no idea what their subscriptions actually cost annually. The average US household now has 7-12 active subscriptions. Netflix + Spotify + iCloud + gym + DashPass + Hulu + Disney+ + ChatGPT Plus can easily total $150-$250/month. The multi-subscription audit is the single most actionable budgeting exercise.
shortcut: Add all your monthly subscriptions, then × 12 for the annual shock number. Round each to the nearest $5 for speed. Drop one? Annual saving = monthly × 12. The real cuts come from the 'I forgot I had this' subscriptions — most households have 2-3.
example:
Real audit (typical household):
Netflix $15 + Spotify $11 + iCloud $3
+ gym $50 + DashPass $10 + ChatGPT $20
+ Hulu $13 + that newsletter $8
= $130/month = $1,560/year

Drop the gym + ChatGPT: save $840/yr
That's a vacation, fully funded.
realWorldHint: Run this once a year to see what your subscriptions actually cost you.

title: Is it actually worth it?
concept: The real cost of anything isn't the sticker price — it's the cost per use. A $120 yoga unlimited pass used 4 times = $30/class (worse than drop-in). A $200 espresso machine used 300 times = $0.67/cup (way better than café). Cost-per-use turns 'is this a good deal?' into a calculation.
shortcut: Cost per use = total price ÷ estimated uses. Compare to your alternative. Estimate uses HONESTLY — most people overestimate how often they'll use things. Unlimited yoga at $120: need 8+ classes vs $18 drop-ins.
example:
Yoga unlimited: $120/mo
4 classes → $30/class
12 classes → $10/class
Drop-in: $18 each
Worth it above 7 classes

Espresso machine: $200
300 cups → $0.67/cup
Café: $4.50/cup
Saves $1,149/yr
realWorldHint: Use this before buying the thing you'll 'definitely use all the time.'

title: Tax, totals, and budget checks
concept: Sales tax in the US is usually 6-10% depending on your state. Two things confuse people: applying the tax to the right base, and the asymmetry that subtracting 10% from a budget doesn't give you the pre-tax max. To go from a post-tax budget to pre-tax: divide by (1 + tax%).
shortcut: Adding tax: price × (1 + tax%). Finding pre-tax max from a budget: budget ÷ (1 + tax%) — NOT budget × (1 − tax%). The asymmetry is small but real: $100 budget at 10% tax → max pre-tax is $90.91, not $90.
example:
$40 item, 8% tax:
10% of $40 = $4
Minus 20% = $0.80 off
Tax ≈ $3.20
Total ≈ $43.20

Budget $100, 10% tax:
Max pre-tax = $100 ÷ 1.10 = $90.91
NOT $90 (which gives $99 total)
realWorldHint: Use this to know your real total before you reach the register.

title: The 50/30/20 rule
concept: The simplest budgeting framework that actually works: 50% of after-tax income to needs (rent, food, transport, insurance, minimum debt), 30% to wants (dining out, entertainment, subscriptions), 20% to savings and debt payoff. The math is simple — the insight is most people have never calculated their own ratios.
shortcut: Half / a third / a fifth of take-home. Quick check: take-home × 0.5 = your needs ceiling. If rent alone exceeds that, your budget is structurally stressed.
example:
Take-home: $4,200/month
Needs: $2,100 (50%)
Wants: $1,260 (30%)
Savings: $840 (20%)

Rent of $2,400? Already above 50% — wants or savings must shrink.
realWorldHint: Use this when you set up a monthly budget or get a raise.

title: Daily habits add up
concept: Small daily expenses compound into significant annual numbers. A $5.50 daily coffee = $2,008/year. A $12 daily workday lunch = $3,120/year. This isn't about telling you to cut your coffee — it's about knowing the real annual cost of any daily habit so you can make informed choices. Some daily habits are worth it. Some aren't. The math helps you decide.
shortcut: Daily × 365 for every-day habits. Workday × 260 for workday-only habits. Want weekly? × 7. Round up for budgeting. Apply this to ANY daily habit — coffee, parking, lunch, snacks, gas — to see its true annual cost.
example:
Annual cost of daily habits:
Coffee $5.50 × 365 = $2,008/yr
Lunch $12 × 260 (workdays) = $3,120/yr
Gas station snack $3 × 260 = $780/yr
Bottled water $2 × 365 = $730/yr

Which are worth it? Your call.
Now you know the real cost.
realWorldHint: Run this when a small daily habit makes you wonder where your money goes.

title: Why your budget is always short
concept: Multiplying weekly cost by 4 gives you a 48-week year — you're missing 4 weeks of expenses annually. A $85/week grocery budget × 4 = $340/month, but the real monthly figure is $85 × 4.33 = $368. Over a year, the wrong multiplier underestimates by ~$336.
shortcut: Weekly × 4.33 (= 52 ÷ 12) for monthly. Biweekly × 2.17 (= 26 ÷ 12). Always round up if budgeting. Monthly → weekly: ÷ 4.33.
example:
Weekly grocery: $85
Wrong (×4): $340/month
Right (×4.33): $368/month

Annual shortfall from ×4: $85 × 52 − ($340 × 12) = $4,420 − $4,080 = $340/year

Biweekly pay $1,800:
Monthly = $1,800 × 2.17 = $3,906
realWorldHint: Use this when a weekly expense quietly blows your monthly budget.

title: Needs vs wants — the line is fuzzier than you think
concept: The 50/30/20 rule only works if you correctly classify your spending. The trap: most people quietly upgrade 'wants' into 'needs' (subscriptions, gym, takeout) and then wonder why they're always over budget. Real needs are non-negotiable bills you can't skip without consequence — rent, basic groceries, utilities, insurance, work transport, debt minimums.
shortcut: Litmus test: 'If I lost my job tomorrow, would I cancel this immediately?' If yes, it's a want. If no (rent, insurance, debt minimums, basic food), it's a need. Streaming, gym, dining out, premium subscriptions = wants, no matter how routine they feel.
example:
Common miscategorizations:
Gym ($40/mo) → want
Spotify + Netflix ($25/mo) → wants
5 dinners out/mo → want
Groceries → need (basic), want (specialty)

When needs exceed 50%:
Rent alone at 40% leaves only 10% for everything else (utilities, food, insurance). Either shrink housing or cut into wants/savings.
realWorldHint: Use this when you're trimming your budget and deciding what's truly essential.

title: Sinking funds — why irregular expenses break your budget
concept: The reason most monthly budgets fail isn't poor discipline — it's irregular expenses. Wedding gifts, holiday spending, vacation, car maintenance, pet vet visits, annual insurance premiums, and birthday gifts all hit unpredictably and turn into 'this month was just expensive' months. A **sinking fund** is a dedicated savings bucket you contribute to every month for a KNOWN future irregular expense, so when it hits you have the cash already saved instead of breaking your budget or going into credit-card debt. The math: monthly contribution = expected total ÷ months until needed. Holidays $1,200 by December? Start in January, $100/month. Vacation $3,000 in June? If it's January, that's $500/month for 6 months. Most adults benefit from 4-6 sinking funds running simultaneously: a Holiday Fund (Nov-Dec), a Travel Fund (whenever), a Car Maintenance Fund (ongoing $50-100/mo), a Pet Fund (ongoing if you have pets), a Gift Fund (birthdays + weddings + baby showers), and sometimes an Annual Insurance / Annual Subscription fund for those bills that arrive once a year. The combined monthly outlay typically lands $200-500 — but it replaces the $1,500-3,000 'surprise spending' months that wreck the budget twice a year.
shortcut: Monthly sinking fund = expected expense ÷ months until needed. Round up. Run 4-6 funds simultaneously in a single HYSA with sub-accounts (most online HYSAs support 'buckets' or 'goals'). Audit them in January: which fund needs more? Which can be cut? The point isn't perfection — it's converting irregular shocks into a predictable monthly line that fits the 50/30/20 budget.
example:
Sample sinking-fund setup, started January, audited in January next year:

  Holiday Fund: $1,200 ÷ 11 months → $110/mo (cuts off Nov)
  Travel Fund: $3,600 ÷ 12 months → $300/mo (replenishes after each trip)
  Car Maintenance: $1,000 ÷ 12 → $85/mo (oil changes + tires + unexpected)
  Gift Fund: $600 ÷ 12 → $50/mo (Mother's Day, birthdays, baby showers)
  Annual Auto Insurance: $1,400 ÷ 12 → $120/mo (paid annually saves ~5% vs monthly)

  Total monthly sinking outlay: $665/mo
  Sounds like a lot — but it REPLACES $1,200 in December credit card debt + a $3,600 vacation that hit savings + four other 'oh I forgot about X' months.

The 50/30/20 rule treats sinking funds as part of the 'needs' bucket (predictable known expense) — not the 'wants' bucket (discretionary). Mis-classifying them is one of the most common reasons people's budgets feel structurally broken every couple of months.

Common failure mode: starting all 5 funds at once with no buffer, going negative on the first big hit. Better: start one fund (Holiday is the easiest 'win'), get to a full year of contributions, then add another. The behavioral momentum matters more than mathematical optimization.
realWorldHint: Set this up so annual bills — insurance, holidays, car registration — never blindside you.

title: Gross vs net — what you actually keep
concept: Your gross pay is what you earn before taxes. Net pay is what arrives in your bank account. Between federal income tax, state tax, Social Security (6.2%), and Medicare (1.45%), most US workers keep roughly 65-80 cents of every dollar earned — the exact share depends on your bracket (per IRS Pub 15) and your state's income tax (zero in TX/FL/WA/NV/AK/SD/TN/WY; 5%+ in CA/NY/NJ/HI). Always plan your budget with net, never gross.
shortcut: Quick estimate: take 25-30% off gross to get net (more in high-tax states, less in no-state-tax states). Earning $3,000/month gross? Expect $2,100-$2,250 net in most states. For annual salary: divide by 12 for monthly gross, then knock off 25-30% for a working budget number.
example:
Gross pay: $3,000/month
FICA (7.65%) + fed (~12%) + state (~5%) ≈ 25%
Net pay ≈ $2,250

$60,000 salary
÷ 12 = $5,000/month gross
In TX (no state tax): ~$3,950 net
In CA (high state tax): ~$3,700 net
realWorldHint: Use this when an offer quotes a salary and you want your real take-home.

title: What a % raise really adds
concept: A percentage raise sounds exciting, but the real number is what lands in your paycheck. A 5% raise on $60,000 is $3,000 more per year — about $250/month before taxes. Knowing the actual dollar impact helps you negotiate and plan clearly.
shortcut: Annual raise = current salary × raise%. Monthly bump = ÷ 12. After-tax: × 0.72 (assumes ~28% total deductions). 5% on $65k = $3,250/yr → $271/mo gross → ~$195/mo in your pocket.
example:
Salary: $60,000
5% raise = $3,000/year
Per month = $250
After tax ≈ $175/month
realWorldHint: Run this the moment you hear your raise number.

title: Overtime pay — time and a half
concept: Federal overtime (FLSA) is 1.5× your regular rate for hours worked beyond 40 in a week — but only for non-exempt employees. Salaried workers who pass the federal exempt threshold and duties test get no OT, no matter how many hours they work. If you're hourly or below the threshold, those extra hours pay significantly more: 8 OT hours at $20/hr earns you $240, not $160. (See lesson 3.9 for exempt vs non-exempt.)
shortcut: Overtime rate = regular × 1.5 (non-exempt only). Overtime pay = OT hours × OT rate. Total week: (40 × regular) + (OT hours × regular × 1.5). At $20/hr (non-exempt) working 47 hours: $800 + (7 × $30) = $1,010 gross.
example:
Regular rate: $20/hr (non-exempt)
Overtime rate: $20 × 1.5 = $30/hr
8 OT hours × $30 = $240
Vs. 8 regular hours = $160
realWorldHint: Use this to check your paycheck added up your overtime correctly.

title: Compare any two paychecks
concept: Job offers come in different pay periods — weekly, bi-weekly, monthly, annual. Bi-weekly is 26 paychecks/year (not 24). To compare any two offers fairly, convert both to annual first. The most expensive mistake: treating bi-weekly as semi-monthly (24 vs 26) — you under-count two paychecks.
shortcut: Annual ÷ 52 = weekly. Annual ÷ 26 = bi-weekly. Annual ÷ 12 = monthly. To compare offers: annualize each, then subtract. $1,150/week vs $4,800/month? $59,800 vs $57,600 — weekly wins by $2,200.
realWorldHint: Use this to compare two jobs that pay on different schedules.

title: Is your raise actually a raise?
concept: A 3% raise sounds great until inflation is 4%. Your purchasing power actually decreased. Real raise = nominal raise − inflation rate. If inflation outpaces your raise, you're effectively taking a pay cut — you can buy less with your new salary than you could before.
shortcut: Real raise % = raise % − inflation %. Real dollar change = salary × real raise %. A 3% raise with 4% inflation: real change = −1%, meaning you lost purchasing power. Always compare your raise to the current inflation rate.
example:
Salary: $65,000
Raise: 3% = $1,950
Inflation: 4% = $2,600
Real change: −$650/year
You're actually losing money
realWorldHint: Run this when your raise arrives to see if you actually came out ahead.

title: Hourly to salary in 2 seconds
concept: Full-time work is roughly 2,000 hours per year (40 hrs × 50 weeks). The mental math: double your hourly rate, add three zeros. $25/hr → double → $50 → add three zeros → $50,000/year. To reverse: drop three zeros, halve. $70,000 → $70 → halve → $35/hr.
shortcut: Hourly to annual: double + three zeros. Annual to hourly: drop three zeros, halve. Works because 2 × 1,000 = 2,000 hours. For part-time, scale: 1,500 hrs = double + 1,500.
example:
Hourly to annual:
$18/hr → $36,000
$32/hr → $64,000

Annual to hourly:
$50,000 → $25/hr
$80,000 → $40/hr

Compare offer:
$28/hr ≈ $56k vs $52k salaried
Hourly wins by $4k
realWorldHint: Use this to instantly translate any hourly rate into a yearly salary.

title: Your salary isn't your compensation
concept: Total compensation = base salary + employer-paid health insurance + 401k match + bonus + stock. For most jobs, total comp is 15-25% higher than base. A $70k base with $8k insurance + $3k match + $5k bonus = $86k total comp. When comparing offers, compare total comp.
shortcut: Add 15-25% to base for a rough total comp estimate. Employer pays $500/mo for your insurance? That's $6k/yr of compensation you never see in your paycheck.
example:
Offer A: $75k base + $6k insurance + $2k match = $83k total
Offer B: $80k base + $3k insurance + $1k match = $84k total

B wins by $1k — barely. A might have better benefits in practice.
realWorldHint: Use this when you're weighing a job offer's full package, not just the salary.

title: Is your side hustle actually worth it?
concept: Effective hourly rate = (earnings − expenses) ÷ total hours including prep, travel, admin. A $200 weekend gig that takes 12 hours and costs $30 in gas is really $14.17/hr — half of what a $28/hr day job pays. Side hustles often look better than they pay.
shortcut: Net earnings ÷ total hours including everything. Compare to your day job hourly equivalent (annual ÷ 2,000). If side hustle pays < 70% of day rate, the time is better spent on rest, a promotion, or a second skill.
example:
Side hustle:
$200 gig
12 hours total
$30 gas
Effective: $14.17/hr

Day job:
$55,000 ÷ 2,000 = $27.50/hr

Gap: $13.33/hr
Side hustle pays 51% of day job — worth it?
realWorldHint: Run this before taking a side gig to see what it really pays per hour.

title: What 'exempt' vs 'non-exempt' actually means
concept: FLSA divides employees into exempt (salaried, no overtime, must pass salary + duties tests) and non-exempt (overtime-eligible at 1.5×). Most people don't know which they are or that misclassification is common. A 2024 DOL rule briefly raised the federal salary threshold to $58,656/year, but federal courts vacated it — and in May 2026 the DOL formally restored the prior regulation, so the enforced federal floor is $35,568/year ($684/week, the 2019 level). Several states (CA, NY, WA) set much higher floors of their own — California's tracks 2× the state minimum wage and rises annually. Always check both federal and state law.
shortcut: Exempt = salary, no overtime; non-exempt = OT-eligible. Below the threshold OR failing the duties test makes you legally non-exempt, whatever HR labels you. States can set higher floors.
example:
Two job offers:
A: $80k exempt salary, expected 50-hour weeks
B: $35/hr non-exempt, 50-hour weeks

A: $80,000/year
B: (40×$35×52) + (10×$35×1.5×52)
  = $72,800 + $27,300 = $100,100/year

Non-exempt wins by $20k if hours are real.
realWorldHint: Check this when a job is 'salaried' and you want to know if you're owed overtime.

title: What does a 401(k) contribution actually cost you?
concept: When you contribute to a traditional (pre-tax) 401(k), the full amount goes into your retirement account but your take-home pay drops by LESS than the full amount — because the contribution also reduces your taxable income. Net paycheck cost = contribution × (1 − your marginal income tax rate). At a 22% bracket, every $100 contributed costs you only $78 in take-home; the IRS effectively pays the other $22 via the tax break (per IRS Pub 525). This is why the headline '6% of salary into 401(k)' feels less painful in practice than the percentage suggests. (Note: FICA still applies to pre-tax 401(k) contributions — see lesson 7.8.)
shortcut: Pre-tax 401(k) net paycheck cost = contribution × (1 − marginal rate). At 22% bracket: $300 contribution costs $234 take-home. At 32% bracket: $300 contribution costs $204 take-home. Higher bracket → contribution feels even cheaper. Roth 401(k) is different: full amount comes out of take-home.
example:
$60,000 salary, 22% federal bracket, 6% contribution rate:
Monthly contribution: $60,000 × 6% ÷ 12 = $300
Income tax saved: $300 × 22% = $66
Real take-home cost: $300 − $66 = $234/month

$60,000 retirement contribution becomes $46,800 in 'real' take-home cost — and the $300/month becomes a 401(k) balance you keep.
realWorldHint: Run this before you set your 401(k) contribution rate.

title: RSUs — what's your stock comp actually worth?
concept: RSUs (Restricted Stock Units) are stock-based compensation. The math most people get wrong: at vest, the shares hit your account AND are taxed as ordinary income at your marginal rate — your employer typically withholds shares to cover the tax at the IRS supplemental withholding rate of 22% (per IRS Pub 15). That rate is too LOW if you're in the 32-37% bracket (above ~$202K single 2026 taxable income, per IRS Rev Proc 2025-32), which means you owe more at tax time than you might expect. Standard tech-industry vest is 4 years with a 1-year cliff: 25% of the grant vests on your first anniversary, then quarterly or monthly until year 4. Each vest is a taxable event AT THAT YEAR'S share price — not at the grant price.
shortcut: Two-step mental on a vest: (1) Gross income added that year = vested shares × current price. (2) Net cash equivalent = vested shares × price × (1 − your marginal rate). For most tech workers in a combined ~32-35% bracket (federal 24% + state 5-13% + FICA Medicare 1.45%): every $10K of RSU vest nets ~$6.5-7K. The 22% IRS supplemental withholding can leave you owing 10-15% more at tax time — set aside the gap.
example:
Alex receives a 4-year RSU grant of 1,000 shares (25% / year), at a grant-date share price of $40.

Year 1 vest (250 shares):
  Stock price now: $50 (up 25%)
  Gross income added: 250 × $50 = $12,500
  Marginal rate (24% fed + 5% state ≈ 29% total): tax owed = $3,625
  Net cash equivalent: $12,500 − $3,625 = $8,875

Year 2 vest (250 shares):
  Stock price now: $60
  Gross: 250 × $60 = $15,000 added to W-2
  Each vest is taxed at THAT year's price, not the grant price.

Underwithholding trap:
  Employer withheld 22% of $12,500 = $2,750
  Actual tax owed at marginal rate: $3,625
  Gap owed at tax time: $875
realWorldHint: Use this when an offer includes stock and you need its real value.

title: W-2 vs 1099 offer — is $50/hr 1099 better than $40/hr W-2?
concept: Two offers, same headline number, different real value. A 1099 contractor role pays a gross hourly rate but you lose: (1) employer FICA half (~7.65%, per IRS — you pay it as self-employment tax instead), (2) employer-sponsored health insurance (~$400-700/month value), (3) employer 401(k) match (typically 3-6% of salary), (4) paid time off (~10-20 days/year = ~5-8% of salary), (5) employer-paid disability + life insurance, (6) the IRS Schedule SE deduction that smooths it (you deduct the employer-equivalent half before computing SE tax — effective SE rate ~14.13%, not 15.3%). After accounting for all of that — partially offset by the 20% QBI deduction on self-employment income, made permanent by OBBBA in 2025 — a 1099 rate needs to be roughly **40-45% higher** than the equivalent W-2 hourly to break even on take-home. Quick screening rule for adults considering a 1099 offer: 1099 hourly × 0.70 ≈ what the equivalent W-2 hourly take-home would feel like, after stripping out the missing employer contributions (net of the QBI deduction).
shortcut: 1099-to-W-2 quick screen: 1099 hourly × 0.70 ≈ W-2-equivalent take-home rate. So $50/hr 1099 ≈ $35/hr W-2 once you net out missing benefits + employer FICA half + missing PTO (net of the QBI deduction). To break even with a $40/hr W-2 job, the 1099 offer needs to be roughly $40 ÷ 0.70 ≈ $57/hr. Big multipliers come from health insurance and PTO — if the 1099 includes healthcare via a spouse or marketplace ACA subsidy, the gap shrinks.
example:
Two offers, side by side:

Offer A: W-2, $40/hr × 2,080 hours = $83,200 gross
  Plus benefits: employer health $6K + 401(k) match $2,500 + 15 PTO days (~$4,800 paid time off) + employer FICA half $6,365 paid on your behalf
  Total compensation: ~$103K

Offer B: 1099, $50/hr × 2,080 hours = $104,000 gross
  Minus SE tax (effective 14.13% per IRS Schedule SE): ~$14,695
  Minus health insurance (self-purchased ACA Silver, single 30-yo): ~$5,400/yr after subsidies
  Minus no 401(k) match: $0 (you can open a Solo 401(k) but employer match is gone)
  Minus no PTO: ~$4,000 of unbillable time
  Plus 20% QBI deduction on self-employment income (made permanent by OBBBA 2025): ~+$4,250 in tax saved
  Net realized: ~$84,150

Offer A ($40/hr W-2) still effectively pays MORE than Offer B ($50/hr 1099) once you count the employer benefits Offer A bundles in. The 1099 rate would need to be roughly $57/hr to match.

Quick screen: $50 × 0.70 = $35 W-2-equivalent. Under $40 → A wins (but closer than it looks). Same math applied to a $75/hr 1099: $75 × 0.70 = $52.50 W-2-equivalent → now above $40, so the 1099 pulls ahead.
realWorldHint: Use this when a contract gig pays more per hour and you're tempted to take it.

title: 401(k) vesting — the match you don't actually own yet
concept: Your contributions to a 401(k) are yours immediately (per IRC § 411(a)(11) — employee-deferred amounts are 100% vested at all times). The employer MATCH is the part with strings attached. Common vesting schedules (per IRC § 411(a)(2) and most plan documents): (1) **Cliff vesting** — 0% until you hit a tenure threshold (1-3 years typical), then 100% all at once. Leave before the cliff and you forfeit the entire match. (2) **Graded vesting** — vest in installments (commonly 20% per year of service, fully vested after 5 years; or 25% per year, fully vested after 4). (3) **Immediate vesting** — the match is yours the day it lands (rare for the match; common for safe-harbor plans). Vesting tracks years of service from your hire date — not from when you started contributing. If you leave 11 months into a 1-year cliff plan, you keep $0 of the employer match (you keep all your own contributions). If you leave at 30 months into a 4-year graded plan vesting 25%/yr, you're typically vested at 50% (the prior year's 25% × 2 full years credited).
shortcut: Vested match = total match × (years served ÷ vesting years), capped at 100%. Cliff plans are binary: 0% before the cliff, 100% after. Graded plans scale linearly with year-count. To compute what walking away costs: total accumulated match × (1 − vested %). Always check your plan's vesting schedule before changing jobs — leaving 2 months before a cliff can cost $10K+ in forfeited match. Don't worry about your own contributions — those are 100% yours from day one.
example:
Jamie, $80K salary, 6% employer match capped, $4,800/year in match over 3 years = $14,400 accumulated match.

Scenario A — 1-year cliff plan, leaves at 10 months:
  Vested: 0% of $4,800 = $0
  Forfeited match: $4,800 (less than full match because year-1 contributions are smaller, but they walk with $0 of it)
  Jamie's contributions: still 100% theirs

Scenario B — 4-year graded plan (25%/yr), leaves at 30 months (2.5 years of service):
  Years credited: 2 (most plans credit full years only)
  Vested: 50% of $14,400 = $7,200
  Forfeited: $7,200 (a real cost of moving before the next vesting milestone)
  Pro tip: if Jamie can hold 6 more months, vesting bumps to 75% = $10,800 — staying through the milestone saves ~$3,600.

Scenario C — Immediate vesting (safe-harbor plan):
  Vested: 100% of $14,400 = $14,400
  Forfeited: $0 — Jamie keeps everything.

Rule of thumb when leaving a job: check your vesting schedule before accepting the new offer. A small delay can capture thousands of dollars of match that would otherwise stay with the old employer.
realWorldHint: Check this before you quit a job and possibly walk away from unvested match.

title: Bonus after tax — why your $10K bonus isn't $10K
concept: Your $10K year-end bonus shows up as ~$6,000-7,500 in your bank account, depending on state. Two things to understand: (1) **Federal withholding** on bonuses uses the IRS supplemental rate of **22%** for cumulative supplemental wages up to $1M, then 37% above (per IRS Pub 15). This is just WITHHOLDING — not your actual tax liability. (2) State income tax + FICA (7.65%) also apply. The combined withholding on a typical bonus lands around 30-40% depending on state. Important nuance: 22% federal supplemental is often LOWER than the bonus recipient's actual marginal tax rate. A worker in the 32% bracket gets only 22% federal withheld on the bonus — but owes 32% at tax filing — so they owe ~10% of the bonus at filing. A worker in the 12% bracket gets 22% withheld but owes only 12% — so they get the difference refunded. The 22% rate is a one-size-fits-all default that creates surprises at filing for both ends of the income range.
shortcut: Quick take-home estimate: bonus × (1 − 22% federal supplemental − stateRate − 7.65% FICA). On $10K in TX (0% state): $10K × (1 − 0.22 − 0 − 0.0765) = $7,035. In CA (~9.3% state): $10K × (1 − 0.22 − 0.093 − 0.0765) = $6,105. Quick adjustment for high earners: if your marginal federal bracket is 24/32/35/37%, expect to OWE the difference at filing time (typically $200-2,000 per $10K bonus). Quick adjustment for low earners (12% bracket): you'll get the over-withholding refunded at filing — effectively a forced savings.
example:
Three workers, same $10,000 year-end bonus:

Maya, TX (0% state tax), 22% federal bracket:
  Federal supplemental (22%): −$2,200
  State (0%): $0
  FICA (7.65%): −$765
  **Take-home: $7,035**
  At filing: 22% withholding matches her 22% marginal — no surprise.

Devon, CA (9.3% effective state), 32% federal bracket:
  Federal supplemental (22%): −$2,200
  State (9.3%): −$930
  FICA (7.65%): −$765
  **Take-home: $6,105**
  At filing: 22% federal withholding under-withholds for the 32% marginal bracket → owes ~$1,000 more federal at filing time. Set it aside in the HYSA, don't spend the take-home as if it's final.

Jordan, NJ (~7% effective state), 12% federal bracket:
  Federal supplemental (22%): −$2,200
  State (7%): −$700
  FICA (7.65%): −$765
  **Take-home: $6,335**
  At filing: 22% federal withholding OVER-withholds for the 12% marginal bracket → refunded ~$1,000 federal at filing time. Effectively a forced savings.

Key rule: never spend the full take-home of a bonus on day one. Wait until your tax return runs — if you're in the 24%+ marginal bracket, expect to owe a meaningful chunk back. If you're in the 12% bracket, expect a refund.
realWorldHint: Run this when a bonus is coming so the smaller-than-expected deposit doesn't shock you.

title: The Rule of 72 — when does it double?
concept: The Rule of 72 is a mental math shortcut: divide 72 by the annual interest rate to estimate how many years it takes for money to double. It works for any growth rate — investment returns, debt interest, even inflation.
shortcut: Years to double = 72 ÷ annual rate. At 8%: 72 ÷ 8 = 9 years. At 6%: 72 ÷ 6 = 12 years. At 12%: 72 ÷ 12 = 6 years. Works equally well in reverse: if something doubles in 10 years, the implied rate is ~7.2%.
example:
Savings at 4%/year:
72 ÷ 4 = 18 years to double

Debt at 12%/year:
72 ÷ 12 = 6 years to double
(if you only pay minimums)
realWorldHint: Use this to estimate how fast any investment — or debt — doubles.

title: ROI — the one number that compares anything
concept: Return on investment is the universal scale: what % did you gain relative to what you put in? A kitchen renovation ($15k → $20k home value) is 33% ROI. The S&P 500 has historically returned ~10%/year nominal long-run average (per S&P 500 historical data; ~7%/year after inflation per Robert Shiller's data series) — but any single year ranges from −37% (2008) to +30%+. A $200 course leading to a $5k raise is 2,500% ROI. ROI lets you compare wildly different decisions on the same axis.
shortcut: ROI% = (gain ÷ cost) × 100. Universal comparison: kitchen reno 33%, course 2,500%, S&P long-run ~10%/yr nominal (~7% real). But ROI isn't always the answer — a $3k vacation has 0% financial ROI but priceless life ROI. And the 10% index-fund figure is a multi-decade average — don't assume next year will hit it.
example:
Course: paid $200, got $5,000 raise
ROI = $5,000 ÷ $200 × 100 = 2,500%

Kitchen reno: $15k → $20k home value
ROI = $5,000 ÷ $15,000 × 100 = 33%

S&P 500 historical:
~10%/yr nominal long-run average (1928-2023)
~7%/yr real (after inflation)
Individual year range: −37% to +30%+
realWorldHint: Use this to compare any two investments on the same footing.

title: 401(k) match — free money math
concept: Many employers match your 401(k) contributions up to a percentage of your salary. If your employer matches 50% up to 6% of your salary, and you contribute 6%, they add an extra 3%. Not contributing enough to get the full match is literally leaving free money on the table.
shortcut: Match amount = your contribution × match rate. If you earn $60,000 and contribute 6% ($3,600), a 50% match gives you $1,800 free. Total going into your 401(k): $5,400. Always contribute at least enough to max the match.
example:
Salary: $60,000
You contribute 6% = $3,600
Employer matches 50% = $1,800
Total: $5,400/year
realWorldHint: Run this on day one of a new job so you never leave free match on the table.

title: Roth vs Traditional IRA — the basics
concept: Both IRAs cap at $7,500/year (2026) or $8,600 if you're 50+ (per IRS Notice 2025-67). The mechanical difference: Roth uses after-tax dollars (you pay tax now, withdraw tax-free in retirement); Traditional uses pre-tax dollars (you skip tax now, pay it on withdrawal). Income above $153k single / $242k MFJ phases out direct Roth contributions (per IRS — backdoor Roth still possible). This lesson covers the mechanics math; the decision rules (which to choose) live in the next lesson, 'Roth vs Traditional — the decision.'
shortcut: Roth: contribution comes from your post-tax cash. Traditional: contribution reduces taxable income by the full amount this year. Tax saved on a Traditional contribution = contribution × your marginal rate. Long-term Roth value = contribution × growth multiplier, tax-free; Traditional value = same growth, but taxed on withdrawal at your future rate.
example:
$5,000 contribution at 22% tax bracket:
Roth: $5,000 comes from post-tax cash; you keep all of it tax-free at withdrawal
Traditional: saves $1,100 in taxes this year; you'll owe tax on withdrawals later

$7k/yr × 25 yrs at 8% growth ≈ $510k
Roth: $510k tax-free at withdrawal
Traditional at 24% future bracket: $510k − $122k tax = $388k after-tax
realWorldHint: Use this when you open an IRA and have to pick Roth or Traditional.

title: Roth vs Traditional — the decision
concept: The honest answer to 'Roth or Traditional?' is **you don't know your future tax bracket** — nobody does. Future tax rates depend on your future income, what state you retire in, what RMDs (required minimum distributions starting at age 73, per IRS) push you into, and what Congress does to tax law over the next 30-40 years. The 2017 TCJA bracket structure was made permanent by the OBBBA in 2025, so the old 'rates snap back in 2026' deadline is gone — but a future Congress can still change rates, and your own income and state of residence will shift over a 30-40 year retirement. So the right framing is hedging, not optimization. Three defaults that work for ~70% of users: (1) Early career in the 12-22% federal bracket → **lean Roth** (decades of tax-free growth, low tax cost to lock in). (2) Peak earning in the 24-37% bracket AND expect lower retirement spending → **lean Traditional** (defer to a likely-lower future rate). (3) Genuinely uncertain (most people) → **split** across Roth and Traditional buckets so you can choose which to withdraw from in retirement based on the bracket you're actually in. Income above the Roth IRA phaseout ($153K single / $242K MFJ in 2026, per IRS Notice 2025-67) closes the direct Roth IRA door — backdoor Roth IRA via a non-deductible Traditional contribution remains legal as of 2026, though it's worth checking whether legislative changes have closed it.
shortcut: Capture the employer match first, then: low bracket leans Roth, high bracket expecting lower retirement spending leans Traditional, unsure split 50/50 so you pick at withdrawal.
example:
Three example users, with the honest 'unknown' framing:

28 y/o earning $55K (12% bracket):
More years for tax-free growth; current tax cost low
→ Lean Roth (IRA + Roth 401k if available)
Reality check: if tax brackets rise dramatically, you've locked in today's rate — net win. If brackets fall, you slightly overpaid — net small loss. Roth wins on the downside risk.

42 y/o earning $200K (24% bracket), expects to retire and spend less:
Defer the 24% to a likely-lower future rate
→ Lean Traditional 401k (defer tax), Roth IRA for flexibility
Reality check: if Congress raises rates above 24% in retirement, you'd have preferred Roth — but that's a real risk, not a foregone conclusion.

50 y/o uncertain about retirement spending:
Split. Some Roth, some Traditional.
→ At retirement, choose which bucket to withdraw from year-by-year based on the bracket you're actually in. The 'tax flexibility' is worth more than getting the original allocation perfect.

Not covered here: RMDs kick in at age 73 (Traditional, per SECURE 2.0); Roth has no RMDs during the original owner's lifetime.
realWorldHint: Use this when you're genuinely unsure whether Roth or Traditional fits you.

title: Roth IRA vs Roth 401(k) vs Traditional 401(k) — same word, different account
concept: Three retirement accounts whose overlapping names confuse most adults. (1) **Roth IRA** — INDIVIDUAL account you open at a brokerage. 2026 cap is $7,500/yr ($8,600 if 50+) per IRS Notice 2025-67, COMBINED with any Traditional IRA contributions. Income phaseout above $153K single / $242K MFJ (2026) for direct contribution. Tax-free withdrawals after 59½ + 5-year rule. NO required minimum distributions (RMDs) during the owner's lifetime. (2) **Roth 401(k)** — EMPLOYER-SPONSORED plan, post-tax contributions. 2026 elective deferral cap is $24,500/yr (shared with the Traditional 401(k) bucket at the same employer); the 50+ catch-up adds $8,000, and ages 60-63 get an $11,250 'super catch-up' instead, per SECURE 2.0. NO income phaseout — high earners excluded from Roth IRA can still use Roth 401(k). Employer match ALWAYS goes to the Traditional (pre-tax) 401(k) bucket regardless of where your elective contributions go. RMDs were eliminated in 2024 by SECURE 2.0. (3) **Traditional 401(k)** — same plan, pre-tax contributions, taxed on withdrawal, RMDs at age 73 (per SECURE 2.0). The naming trap: 'Roth' and 'Traditional' describe TAX TREATMENT; 'IRA' and '401(k)' describe ACCOUNT TYPE. They're independent: you can have a Traditional 401(k) at work AND a Roth IRA on the side, with separate caps.
shortcut: Two independent axes: Roth vs Traditional is tax treatment, IRA vs 401(k) is account type. Their caps are separate, not combined, and the employer match always lands pre-tax.
example:
Maya is 32, earning $95K single. Her benefits offer both a Roth 401(k) and a Traditional 401(k). She's also opening an IRA on her own.

Maya's max 2026 contribution capacity:
  401(k) elective deferral: $24,500 (any mix of Roth + Traditional)
  IRA: $7,500 (any mix of Roth + Traditional)
  Total max: $32,000

Maya's setup (her own elections):
  Roth 401(k): $14,000/yr
  Traditional 401(k): $10,500/yr
  Total elective deferral: $24,500 ✓
  Roth IRA at Fidelity: $7,500 (below the $153K single phaseout)

Employer adds:
  50% match up to 6% of $95K = $2,850/yr → goes into the TRADITIONAL 401(k) bucket regardless of where Maya's elective contributions go.

Maya's actual total annual retirement contributions: $32,000 (her) + $2,850 (employer) = $34,850.

Common confusion the lesson prevents:
  'I can contribute $7.5K to my Roth IRA AND $7.5K to my Roth 401(k), right?' → Wrong. The IRA cap is its own thing, but the 401(k) cap ($24,500) is shared across Roth + Traditional within the same employer plan.
  'My Roth 401(k) match grows tax-free, right?' → No. The match goes pre-tax (Traditional) and is taxed at withdrawal — even if your own contributions are Roth.
realWorldHint: Use this when your benefits portal asks you to pick between confusingly-named accounts.

title: Compound growth over time
concept: Compound growth is your money earning money on its earnings. $500/month at 8% grows to $91k in 10 years, $296k in 20, $745k in 30. The longer your time horizon, the more of your final balance is interest (not contributions). Time matters more than amount.
shortcut: Total contributed = monthly × 12 × years. At 8% growth, multiplier is ~1.5× in 10 yrs, ~2.5× in 20, ~4.5× in 30. % of balance that's interest: 33% at 10 yrs, 60% at 20 yrs, 78% at 30 yrs. Start early — every decade roughly doubles your money via compounding.
example:
$500/month × 20 years:
Contributed: $120,000
Grew to: $296,000
Interest: $176,000 (60% of balance)

Start at 25 vs 35 (both stop at 65):
25 → $1.3M
35 → $570k
Gap from 10 years: $730k
realWorldHint: Use this to see what investing today is worth decades from now.

title: Reverse goal — how much per month to hit $1M?
concept: Compound interest is usually taught forward: '$500/month at 8% → $X in N years.' The more practical question is **backward**: 'I want $1M by 65. I'm 30. How much per month?' The exact math is the future-value annuity formula solved for PMT: monthly = goal × (r/12) ÷ ((1 + r/12)^(years × 12) − 1), where r is the annual return as a decimal. Mental approximation that works: at 8% nominal return (a defensible long-run S&P 500 assumption per historical data, ~10% before inflation / ~7% after), every $100/month contributed grows to ~**$150K over 30 years** and ~**$330K over 40 years**. Scale linearly from there: $1M over 30 yrs at 8% ≈ $670/month. $1M over 40 yrs ≈ $300/month. $500K over 25 yrs ≈ $530/month. The takeaway: starting 10 years earlier roughly cuts the required monthly contribution in half — time is mathematically much more powerful than amount for long horizons.
shortcut: Mental anchor table at 8% annual return: $100/mo for 20 yrs → ~$59K · 25 yrs → ~$95K · 30 yrs → ~$150K · 35 yrs → ~$230K · 40 yrs → ~$330K. Scale linearly: $1M at 30 yrs = $1M ÷ $150K × $100/mo ≈ $667/mo. The exact annuity formula is slightly different, but this scaling lands within 3-5% of the precise answer — close enough for goal-setting. To check yourself: monthly × 12 × years × ~3-4 ≈ final value (rough check; the multiplier rises with time horizon).
example:
Three retirement scenarios at 8% nominal expected return:

Ava, age 25, wants $1M by 65 (40-year horizon):
  Mental: $1M ÷ $330K × $100 = $303/mo
  Exact annuity formula: $286/mo
  Within 5% — pick $300/mo and round up.

Marcus, age 35, same goal $1M by 65 (30-year horizon):
  Mental: $1M ÷ $150K × $100 = $667/mo
  Exact: $671/mo
  Within 1% on this one.

Kenji, age 45, $1M by 65 (20-year horizon):
  Mental: $1M ÷ $59K × $100 = $1,695/mo
  Exact: $1,698/mo
  Almost identical.

The big insight: Ava contributes $303/mo × 40 yrs × 12 = $145K total. Kenji contributes $1,698/mo × 20 yrs × 12 = $408K total. Both end at $1M. Ava puts in **$263K less** because of 20 extra years of compounding. This is why 'start early' is the most universally repeated retirement advice — the math actually justifies the cliché.

Quick gut-check rule of thumb (8% nominal, 30 years): every $1M you want in 30 years costs roughly $670/month. Every $100K costs ~$67/month. Adjust for different time horizons using the anchor table above.
realWorldHint: Run this when you have a savings target and need a monthly number to hit it.

title: The power of investing every month
concept: Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) means investing a fixed dollar amount at regular intervals regardless of market conditions. The math story: per Vanguard's 2012 study ("Dollar-Cost Averaging Just Means Taking Risk Later"), lump-sum investing beats DCA roughly two-thirds of the time on returns, because markets go up more often than they go down. The cost of DCA-vs-lump-sum is called the **cash drag** — the foregone return on the money that's still sitting in cash waiting to be invested. Mental approximation: cash drag ≈ total amount × annual return ÷ 2 (because on average the un-invested dollars sit in cash for half the DCA period). On $12K DCA'd over 12 months at an 8% expected market return, the cash drag is roughly $12,000 × 8% ÷ 2 = $480 of foregone return. So why does DCA still win for most people? It wins on **behavior**. Lump-sum requires you to actually invest all at once — most investors who try to time the entry hesitate, wait for a 'better moment,' get scared by a dip, and end up investing less than they intended. DCA removes the decision and the emotion. The $480 cash drag is cheap insurance for the larger risk that you never invest the lump sum at all.
shortcut: DCA cash drag (the expected cost vs lump-sum) ≈ total × expected annual return ÷ 2. At 8% expected return DCAing $12K over 12 months: $12K × 8% ÷ 2 = $480. That's the math premium. The behavioral premium of automated DCA on payday — guaranteed deployment of every dollar — usually exceeds the math premium of theoretical lump-sum. Pick the strategy you'll actually execute. Automated DCA on payday > theoretically-optimal lump-sum you keep delaying.
example:
Lump-sum vs DCA (Vanguard 2012 study):
  Lump-sum wins on returns ~67% of the time over 10-year windows.
  But: lump-sum requires investing all at once, which most retail investors don't actually do.

Real-world outcomes:
  Investor A: $12k DCA'd over 12 months → invested all $12k. Cash drag: $12K × 8% ÷ 2 = $480 of foregone return vs ideal lump-sum.
  Investor B: planned $12k lump-sum → kept waiting for a dip → invested $4k over 18 months. Effective 'cash drag' of un-invested $8K plus actual missed-market return ≈ $1,500+.
  Investor A wins by $1,000+ despite the lower theoretical expected return.

The right rule: if the money came in as a lump (bonus, inheritance) AND you'd otherwise let it sit in checking >3 months, lump-sum the moment you have it. Otherwise automate the DCA and stop thinking about it.
realWorldHint: Use this when you're deciding whether to invest a little every month.

title: APY — making your savings work
concept: APY (Annual Percentage Yield) is the savings-side counterpart to APR — it's the simple rate WITH compounding included. Where APR is what you pay on debt, APY is what you earn on savings. The math: APY = (1 + r/n)^n − 1, where r is the nominal rate and n is the compounding periods per year. In practice, the difference between APR and APY at typical rates is small (4% APR with monthly compounding ≈ 4.07% APY). What matters more is the rate gap between accounts: a big-bank savings account at 0.01% APY vs a high-yield savings account (HYSA) at 4-5% APY differs by ~500× on the same balance. Federal law (Truth in Savings Act / Reg DD, per FDIC) requires banks to disclose APY on savings products, which makes APY the right comparison number across savings accounts, CDs, and money market funds.
shortcut: Annual interest earned = balance × APY. Monthly interest ≈ balance × APY ÷ 12. Doubling time = 72 ÷ APY (Rule of 72 reuse). For typical rates, APR and APY differ by < 0.1 percentage points — but the gap between a 0.01% big-bank savings account and a 4.5% HYSA is enormous ($1 vs $450 per year on $10k).
example:
$10,000 in three different accounts (1 year):

Big-bank savings (0.01% APY): $1 earned
Money market fund (4.5% APY): $450 earned
HYSA (4.5% APY): $450 earned
5-yr CD (4.7% APY): $470 earned (locked up)

The difference between '0.01%' and '4.5%' is 450× — far bigger than any small APR-vs-APY compounding adjustment. The first action for anyone with idle cash above their checking buffer: move it to an HYSA.
realWorldHint: Run this before you leave cash in a big-bank account paying almost nothing.

title: ESPP — is your company stock purchase plan free money?
concept: An ESPP (Employee Stock Purchase Plan) under IRC § 423 lets you buy company stock at a discount, typically 15% off (max allowed by code) with a 'lookback' provision that uses the LOWER of the start-of-period or end-of-period share price. Qualified plans cap purchases at $25,000 of fair-market-value stock per calendar year (per IRC § 423). The math that makes ESPP a near-guaranteed win: on a 15% discount, immediate sale locks in 15 / (100 − 15) = 17.6% gain on every dollar contributed. Over a typical 6-month offering period, that's roughly a 38% annualized return on the cash that cycled through. The trap most people miss: holding too much company stock concentrates your risk (your salary AND your savings are tied to one employer's stock price). The standard advice — 'always max ESPP if you can spare the contribution AND will sell immediately' — assumes you'll diversify the proceeds, not accumulate them.
shortcut: Immediate-sale guaranteed gain = contribution × discount / (100 − discount). At 15% discount: every $1 in produces ~$0.176 of immediate gain. Annualized for a 6-month period: ~38% APY on the cycling cash. The mental rule: max contribution if you can spare 5-15% of pay AND will quick-flip the shares on purchase day. Federal cap: $25K of FMV/yr (per IRC § 423). Note: short-term capital gains tax applies on the discount portion if you sell within 1 year of purchase (or 2 years from grant).
example:
Mia contributes $5,000 to her ESPP over a 6-month offering period. 15% discount, lookback feature.

Scenario A (flat price, $50 → $50):
  Purchase price = $50 × 85% = $42.50
  Shares bought: $5,000 ÷ $42.50 = 117.6 shares
  Immediate sale at $50: 117.6 × $50 = $5,882
  Gain: $882 (17.6% on the contribution)
  Annualized (6 months): ~38%

Scenario B (lookback bonanza, $50 → $80):
  Lookback uses lower price ($50), so purchase still at $42.50
  Shares: 117.6
  Immediate sale at $80: 117.6 × $80 = $9,408
  Gain: $4,408 (88% — combined discount + run-up)
  The lookback turns a great deal into a spectacular one when the stock runs.

Federal cap reminder: $25K of FMV stock purchases per year (per IRC § 423). Many plans cap participation at 10-15% of salary which keeps most workers under that anyway.
realWorldHint: Use this when your company offers a stock purchase plan and you're unsure it's worth it.

title: The fee that eats your retirement
concept: A 1% expense ratio sounds small. On $100k it's $1,000/year — but the real cost is the compounding you lose. Over 30 years at 8% growth, that 1% fee costs you roughly $200,000 in lost final balance. The gap between a 0.03% index fund and a 1% managed fund is staggering.
shortcut: Annual fee = portfolio × expense ratio. Quick rule: every 0.5% in fees costs about 10% of your final balance over 30 years. Choose funds with expense ratios under 0.2% wherever possible.
example:
$100k portfolio, 1% expense ratio:
Annual fee: $1,000

$200k portfolio, 0.5% vs 0.05%:
Diff: 0.45% × $200k = $900/yr
Over 30 yrs ≈ $50k+ lost

Always check expense ratios.
realWorldHint: Check this before picking a fund — a small fee quietly costs you a fortune.

title: How much emergency fund do you actually need?
concept: 3-6 months of ESSENTIAL expenses — not income. Essential means rent, food, insurance, transport, debt minimums. Not subscriptions, dining out, entertainment. Most people calculate against income and get an overwhelming number; calculating against essentials makes the goal achievable.
shortcut: Sum your 4-5 non-negotiable monthly bills. That's your essential number. × 3 = minimum target, × 6 = solid. Months of runway = current savings ÷ essentials. Cut $X from non-essentials = (savings ÷ (essentials − cut)) months of runway.
example:
Essentials:
Rent $1,500 + food $400 + insurance $200 + transport $200 + debt min $300 = $2,600/month

Target (6 months): $15,600
You have $9,800 saved.
Runway: $9,800 ÷ $2,600 = 3.8 months
realWorldHint: Use this before life throws a job loss or surprise bill at you.

title: Where should your emergency fund actually sit?
concept: Knowing you need 3-6 months of essentials is only half the answer. The other half: where does it live? The wrong place either loses you ~$1,000+/year in foregone interest (sitting in a 0.01% APY big-bank savings account) OR locks you out of accessing it when you need it (a 5-year CD with early-withdrawal penalty). The right place depends on the size of your fund. **Decision tree by balance:** (1) **Under $1,000 starter EF** → leave it in checking as a buffer (per the r/personalfinance Order of Operations). Liquidity beats yield at this scale. (2) **$1K to ~$30K full EF** → high-yield savings account (HYSA) at ~4-4.5% APY, FDIC-insured. Vanguard / Ally / Marcus / Discover / SoFi / Wealthfront all in this range. (3) **Above ~$30K** → split across multiple FDIC-insured banks ($250K limit per depositor per bank, per FDIC) OR use a fintech with a sweep network OR use short-term US Treasury bills (similar yield, state-tax-free, backed by US government, ~4% in 2026). (4) **Bonus tier** → for a portion you're confident you won't touch in 6+ months, a no-penalty CD or short-duration T-bill can pick up 25-50 basis points more — but never your full EF.
shortcut: Rank your EF home in this order: liquidity first (accessible in 1-2 days, no penalties), yield second (move it to a HYSA), insurance third (split across banks or use T-bills above the $250K FDIC limit).
example:
Three realistic EF scenarios:

Maya, age 26, just started saving:
  EF size: $800 (building toward $1K starter)
  Right home: checking account, $800 buffer
  Wrong move: any kind of HYSA hassle for $800 isn't worth it yet.

Taylor, age 32, established EF:
  EF size: $18,000 (6 months of $3K essentials)
  Right home: HYSA at 4.5% APY → $810/year in interest, fully liquid
  Wrong moves: leaving it in 0.01% big-bank savings ($1.80/yr); locking $10K of it in a 1-year CD with early-withdrawal penalty; putting it in an index fund (could be down 30% the day you need it).
  The right move earns ~$800/yr in passive interest with no liquidity sacrifice.

Jordan, age 45, family of four, larger EF:
  EF size: $60,000 (9 months at $6,700 essentials)
  Right home: $50K in primary HYSA + $10K in a secondary FDIC bank (or a fintech sweep network). At the FDIC limit ($250K) consider 4-week T-bills via TreasuryDirect — same yield, state-tax-free, no FDIC-limit ceiling.
  Wrong moves: $60K at one bank below the FDIC limit is fine but inflexible if rates diverge between banks. Some Fintech 'high yield' accounts have hidden requirements (direct deposit / transaction count) that drop yield to near-zero if you don't comply.

What NOT to use as EF: 401(k) (taxes + penalty + lockup), brokerage taxable accounts holding equities (market loss risk), CDs longer than 6 months (early-withdrawal penalty), real estate equity, crypto.
realWorldHint: Use this to decide where your emergency cash should actually live.

title: Rental property — does it actually cash-flow?
concept: A rental property's 'yield' is a marketing number. The real question is whether the property cash-flows after all real costs — and most don't. To assess honestly, subtract from monthly rent: mortgage P&I, property taxes (~1-2% of price ÷ 12, varies by state per Tax Foundation), insurance, HOA, vacancy reserve (~8% of rent), maintenance reserve (~10% of rent), capex reserve (~5-10% of rent), and management (~10% of rent if you hire it out). What's left is real cash flow. The famous '1% rule' (monthly rent ≥ 1% of purchase price) IS the canonical back-of-envelope sanity check — but it's materially stale in major-metro markets. In SF, NYC, LA, Boston, San Diego, and Seattle, rent-to-price ratios have been below 0.5% since the mid-2010s (per Apartment List + Zumper city rent data); virtually no property there meets the 1% rule. Properties in those markets can still cash-flow positive through appreciation + tax benefits + leverage, but the cash-flow analysis below tells you that — the 1% rule alone doesn't. Use the 1% rule as a screen in Midwest / Sun Belt / lower-cost-of-living markets; in high-cost-of-living metros, go straight to the full cash-flow line items.
shortcut: Rent under 1% of price rarely cash-flows — and even at 1%, check it's positive after the mortgage and real reserves. Banking on appreciation isn't investing, it's speculating.
example:
$300k property, $2,200/month rent (passes 1% rule barely):

Income:        $2,200
Mortgage P&I:  −$1,400 (20% down, 7% rate, 30 yr)
Property tax:  −$250
Insurance:     −$100
Vacancy 8%:    −$175
Maintenance:   −$220
Capex reserve: −$165
Management:    −$220
────────────────
Real cash flow: −$330/month

'8% gross yield' becomes negative cash flow when you account for everything. This is why most first-time landlords are surprised.

Metro-market reality check: same calc on a $1.2M SF condo renting for $4,500/month. Rent-to-price ratio is 0.375% — way under the 1% threshold. After expenses, cash flow is roughly −$2,500/month. SF investors run a different math: they accept negative cash flow expecting appreciation + leveraged equity build to make the long-term IRR work. That's a real strategy, but the lesson is they're NOT investing for cash flow — they're investing for appreciation, which is a different bet with different risk.
realWorldHint: Run this before you buy a rental expecting it to cash-flow.

title: Am I on track? The retirement savings check
concept: Fidelity's age-based rule: 1× salary saved by 30, 3× by 40, 6× by 50, 10× by 67. Calculate your 'savings multiple' (current savings ÷ current salary) and compare to your age target. If behind, increase your contribution by 1% of salary each year until you catch up.
shortcut: Multiple = savings ÷ salary. Age 30 target = 1×. Age 35 = 2×. Age 40 = 3×. Gap (in dollars) = (target multiple × salary) − current savings. Monthly to close in N years = gap ÷ (N × 12).
example:
Age 35, salary $65k, saved $80k:
Multiple = $80k ÷ $65k = 1.23×
Target at 35: ~2×
Gap: (2 × $65k) − $80k = $50k

Close in 5 years: $50k ÷ 60 months = $833/mo extra savings
realWorldHint: Use this to check whether your retirement savings fit your age.

title: Stocks, bonds, index funds — what they actually are
concept: Most adults invest in a 401k without knowing what each option actually IS. Stock = partial ownership in a company. Bond = a loan you made to a company or government, repaid with interest. Index fund = a basket holding all stocks in a market index (like the S&P 500). ETF and mutual fund are different wrappers around the same idea — ETFs trade like stocks all day, mutual funds settle once daily at close.
shortcut: Just buy the market: an index fund (or a target-date fund that auto-adjusts as you age) beats ~85-95% of active US large-cap managers over 20-year windows. Stock = ownership; bond = a loan.
example:
Risk/return ranking (historical):
Individual stock > Index fund > Bond > Savings account

For most people: a target-date fund is the right default. It's diversified, low-fee, and auto-rebalances. The S&P 500 has averaged ~10%/year nominal long-run returns (per S&P historical data) — versus most active managers who can't beat it net of fees (per SPIVA).
realWorldHint: Use this the first time you stare at your 401(k)'s fund options and feel lost.

title: Asset allocation: stocks vs bonds by age
concept: How you split between stocks (growth, volatility) and bonds (stability, lower return) matters more than which specific funds you pick. Two separate things drive the right mix: **risk capacity** (how long until you need the money — long horizons can absorb crashes) and **risk tolerance** (how you actually behave when the market drops 30%). The famous '120 minus your age' rule is a starting point, not gospel — Vanguard and Fidelity both now suggest more equity exposure than the older '100 minus your age' rule because lifespans are longer. Use the rule as a default; let your tolerance push you ± 10-20%.
shortcut: Default to stocks % ≈ 110-120 minus your age, then adjust for nerve: dial down 10-20% if you'd panic-sell in a 30% drop, up if you'd treat a crash as a buying opportunity.
example:
Age 28, retirement ~40 yrs away:
Default (110-age): ~82% stocks · (120-age): ~92% stocks
Both defensible; depends on tolerance.

Age 28 with 60% bonds: too conservative — gives up decades of compounding to avoid volatility you have time to ride out.
Age 55 with 100% stocks: too aggressive — a major crash within 10 years of retirement is hard to recover from on a fixed timeline.
realWorldHint: Use this to decide how much of your portfolio should be stocks vs bonds.

title: Why you panic-sell (and how to stop)
concept: The math of investing is simple. The behavior is hard. Loss aversion (losses hurt ~2× more than equivalent gains feel good, per Kahneman & Tversky's prospect theory research), recency bias (recent events feel like they'll continue forever), and herd behavior (selling because everyone else is) destroy returns. Investors who sold during the March 2020 COVID crash missed a recovery that took the S&P 500 from its March 23 low back to its February high by August 2020, and ~70% above the low by year-end (per S&P 500 historical data).
shortcut: Two rules that beat 95% of behavioral mistakes: (1) Automate contributions on payday so you can't 'wait for a better moment.' (2) Don't check your balance during a crash — checking triggers panic, panic triggers selling, selling locks in losses.
example:
March 2020 COVID crash (S&P 500):
Dropped ~34% over Feb 19 - Mar 23, 2020.
Recovered to pre-crash high by August 2020.
By Dec 31, 2020: ~+70% from the March 23 low.

Panic-sellers in March locked in 34% losses. Holders who did nothing watched their accounts surpass all-time highs within a year. The behavioral discipline was worth more than any stock pick.
realWorldHint: Remember this the next time the market drops and you want to sell everything.

title: How credit card interest works
concept: Credit card APR sounds small — 20% — but it compounds. As a mental approximation, the monthly interest charge ≈ balance × APR ÷ 12. Real billing is slightly different: most US issuers use the 'average daily balance' method with a daily periodic rate of APR ÷ 365 (per CFPB Credit Card Agreement standards), so balances that fluctuate within the month produce a slightly different exact charge — your card's exact formula is spelled out in your cardholder agreement, so check your statement to confirm. For sanity-checking, the APR ÷ 12 mental model lands within a few dollars on typical balances.
shortcut: Mental estimate: monthly interest ≈ balance × APR ÷ 12. To compute: move the decimal left two places to get 1%, multiply by your APR, divide by 12. $2,000 × 20% ÷ 12 = $33.33/month. Real issuer billing (daily periodic rate × average daily balance) lands within ~$1-2 of this.
example:
Balance: $2,000 · APR: 20%
Monthly approximation: 20% ÷ 12 = 1.67%
Interest ≈ $2,000 × 1.67% = $33.33

Real billing on a stable balance: identical.
Real billing on a balance that swung from $1,500 → $2,500 mid-month: based on average daily balance ≈ $2,000 — still ~$33.
realWorldHint: Use this to sanity-check the interest charge on your card statement.

title: The minimum payment trap
concept: Older guides taught a flat '2% of balance' minimum, but most US issuers actually calculate it as roughly 1% of your principal + this month's interest charge + any fees, with a $25-$35 floor on tiny balances. Your issuer's exact formula varies — check your statement or cardholder agreement to confirm. That formula keeps you barely treading water — most of every minimum payment goes to interest, not what you owe. Issuers designed it that way: minimums are profitable for them.
shortcut: Realistic minimum ≈ (balance × 1%) + (balance × APR ÷ 1200). On $3,000 at 20% APR: $30 + $50 = $80/month (not the $60 the old 2% rule suggests). Floor: $25-35 for small balances. Always pay above the minimum — even +$50/month cuts years off payoff.
example:
Balance: $3,000 at 20% APR
1% of balance = $30 (principal)
+ monthly interest = $3,000 × 20% ÷ 12 = $50
= $80 minimum

Of that $80, only $30 reduces what you owe — the other $50 is pure interest.
realWorldHint: Use this when you're tempted to just pay the minimum on your card.

title: The true cost of a loan
concept: The sticker price of a loan is not what you pay. Total = monthly payment × number of months. The difference between that and your original loan is the lender's profit — pure interest. The 'interest tax' = total interest ÷ loan amount. Above 15%? Question whether you really need to borrow.
shortcut: Total cost = payment × months. Interest = total − loan. Interest tax % = interest ÷ loan × 100. A $6k loan costing $1,200 interest = 20% interest tax. Save and pay cash if you can spread the wait over 12 months.
example:
Loan: $6,000
Payment: $200/month × 36 months
Total: $7,200
Interest: $1,200
Interest tax: 20%

Save $250/month for 24 months:
You'd have $6,000 cash, save $1,200
realWorldHint: Run this before you sign any loan to see what it really costs.

title: Debt-to-income ratio
concept: DTI ratio = total monthly debt payments ÷ monthly income × 100. Lenders use this to assess risk. Under 36% is healthy; over 43% is a red flag for mortgage approval. It tells you how much of your income is already spoken for.
shortcut: DTI% = monthly debt ÷ monthly income × 100. If you earn $5,000/month and pay $1,500 in debt: $1,500 ÷ $5,000 × 100 = 30% DTI. Keep it under 36%.
example:
Monthly income: $5,000
Debt payments: $1,500
DTI = $1,500 ÷ $5,000 × 100 = 30%
realWorldHint: Use this before applying for a mortgage or car loan.

title: The power of extra payments
concept: Every extra dollar you pay toward debt does two things: kills the interest that dollar would have generated this year, AND shrinks the principal so every future month accrues less interest too. The first-year saving (~extra × APR%) is just the floor — the cumulative saving over the full payoff window is several multiples larger because each smaller balance keeps compounding less.
shortcut: First-year interest saved ≈ extra payment × APR%. Cumulative saving over the full payoff is typically 2-4× that, depending on how long until payoff. On 20% APR debt: $100/mo extra saves ~$240 in year 1, but ~$600-1,200 over a 3-5 year payoff (the principal shrinks each month, so future interest shrinks with it).
example:
Extra: $100/mo · APR: 20%
Year 1 interest saved: ~$240 ($100 × 20% × 12)

Full payoff (~3 yrs on a $3k balance):
Total interest saved: ~$700
Reason: each $100 of extra principal kills not just its own 20% APR, but every future month's interest on that $100 too.
realWorldHint: Run this to see how much faster a little extra each month clears your debt.

title: How long until you're debt-free?
concept: Most r/personalfinance posters asking 'when will I be out of debt?' don't realize how long fixed-monthly-payment payoff actually takes at credit-card APRs. The math is exponential because each month's interest is computed on the remaining balance. A $5,000 balance at 22% APR with $150/month payments takes about 52 months (4⅓ years); bump that payment to $200/month and you finish in about 34 months (under 3 years) — an 18-month reduction. The shortcut: net principal reduction per month = payment − (balance × APR ÷ 1200). Once you see how little of a minimum payment touches principal, the case for paying above-minimum becomes obvious.
shortcut: Net principal reduction = monthly payment − (balance × APR ÷ 1200). If that number is small (e.g. $25 on a $5k balance), payoff takes years. Rule of thumb: every extra $50/month on a $5k balance at 22% APR cuts roughly 15-18 months off the payoff. Step one is always understanding what fraction of your payment is actually shrinking what you owe.
example:
$5,000 balance at 22% APR:
Monthly interest charge = $5,000 × 22% ÷ 12 ≈ $92

Payment $150/mo:
  Principal reduced this month: $150 − $92 = $58
  Payoff time: ~52 months (~4⅓ years)

Payment $200/mo:
  Principal reduced: $200 − $92 = $108
  Payoff time: ~34 months (~2 yrs 10 mo)

The extra $50/month cuts 18 months off the payoff — because every dollar of extra principal also reduces every future month's interest charge.
realWorldHint: Use this to see exactly when your card balance hits zero.

title: Balance transfer — is the 0% APR worth the fee?
concept: A balance transfer moves your credit card balance to a card offering 0% APR for an introductory window (typically 12, 15, 18, or 21 months — per major issuers' published terms). The catch: the new card charges a one-time fee, typically 3-5% of the transferred balance. The math: it's worth it if (balance × old APR × promo months ÷ 12) > (balance × fee%). In dollar form: interest you would have paid during the promo period > transfer fee. The key trap: this only works if you ACTUALLY pay off the balance during the promo window — otherwise you're back to high APR on the new card after the intro period ends.
shortcut: Quick test: is your old APR × (promo months ÷ 12) > the fee %? At 22% APR with a 15-month promo: 22% × 1.25 = 27.5% of interest avoided vs 3-5% fee — strong yes. At lower APRs or shorter promos: do the math. Always plan to pay off before the promo ends — set the monthly payment = balance ÷ promo months minimum.
example:
$8,000 balance at 22% APR · 18-month 0% promo · 3% transfer fee:

Fee = $8,000 × 3% = $240
Interest avoided (18 months at 22%):
  $8,000 × 22% × 18/12 = $2,640

Net benefit: $2,640 − $240 = +$2,400

Monthly payment needed to clear before promo ends:
$8,000 ÷ 18 = ~$445/month
If you can't sustain that, the transfer might still help, but the math gets less favorable when the leftover balance hits the new card's regular APR.
realWorldHint: Run this before moving a balance to a 0% card with a transfer fee.

title: Credit card rewards vs interest — when 2% cashback is meaningless
concept: The marketing copy on every cashback / points card assumes you pay your statement balance in full each month. The math is simple: 2% on $1,000/month spend = $20/month in rewards = $240/year. That's real money — if you carry $0 balance. But the moment you carry a balance, the APR almost always swamps the rewards. A 22% APR on a $1,000 carried balance costs ~$18/month in interest — wiping out the $20 in rewards for $2/month of net 'win.' Carry $3,000 at 22%: interest is $55/month, rewards still $20, net loss is $35/month or $420/year. The marketing implication that 'cashback offsets your spending' is technically true *only* if you pay in full. For anyone carrying a balance, optimizing for cashback is mathematically backwards — the right card is one with the LOWEST APR, not the highest rewards. The break-even balance (the carried balance at which rewards equal interest) = monthly spend × cashback% × 12 ÷ APR. On $1,000/mo spend at 2% rewards and 22% APR: break-even balance = $1,000 × 2% × 12 ÷ 22% ≈ $1,091. Carry more than that and rewards are net-negative.
shortcut: Net rewards (monthly) = (monthly spend × cashback%) − (carried balance × APR ÷ 1200). On $1K/mo spend, 2% cashback, $0 balance: +$20/mo win. With $5K carried at 22%: $20 − $92 = −$72/mo net LOSS. Always: only chase rewards if you pay statement balance in full. If you carry a balance, dump the rewards card and get a low-APR card or balance-transfer card (see lesson on balance transfers).
example:
Three users with the same 2% cashback card on $1,500/month spend:

Alex — pays in full every month:
  Monthly rewards: $1,500 × 2% = $30
  Monthly interest: $0
  Net win: +$30/mo = +$360/year
  Rewards are real money for Alex.

Jordan — carries $2,000 balance at 22% APR:
  Monthly rewards: $30
  Monthly interest: $2,000 × 22% ÷ 12 = $36.67
  Net loss: −$6.67/mo = −$80/year
  Rewards no longer pay for themselves.

Casey — carries $6,000 balance at 24% APR:
  Monthly rewards: $30
  Monthly interest: $6,000 × 24% ÷ 12 = $120
  Net loss: −$90/mo = −$1,080/year
  Casey is being misled by the marketing — switching to a 15% APR card (lower rewards or no rewards) saves more than the cashback would ever earn.

Break-even balance for Alex's card (2% rewards, 22% APR): $1,500 × 2% × 12 ÷ 22% ≈ $1,636. If Alex carries less, rewards win; carry more, interest wins. Simple test: is your carried balance bigger than the break-even? Then your 'rewards card' is costing you money every month.
realWorldHint: Remember this before chasing cashback while carrying a balance.

title: Statement close vs due date — why timing your payment matters
concept: Every credit card has three dates that matter: (1) **Statement close date** — the day your balance is snapshotted and reported to the three credit bureaus (Experian, Equifax, TransUnion). (2) **Payment due date** — typically 21-25 days after statement close (the federal-law-minimum grace period, per CARD Act of 2009 / Reg Z). (3) **The gap between them** — your grace period, which protects you from interest on new purchases but does NOT change what utilization gets reported. The mistake nearly everyone makes: paying just before the due date doesn't help your reported utilization. Credit bureaus see your balance as of the STATEMENT CLOSE, not as of payment. So if you charge $4,500 on a $5,000-limit card and pay it off on the due date, your card issuer still reports 90% utilization for that month — even though you paid in full. To minimize reported utilization, pay BEFORE the statement closes, not just before the due date.
shortcut: Two payment rules. (1) Avoid interest: pay statement balance in full BY the due date — that's what the grace period exists for. (2) Optimize utilization for credit-score purposes: pay BEFORE the statement closes so the bureau sees a low balance. To find your statement close date: log into your card's online portal — it's on the statement page (sometimes called 'cycle close' or 'billing period end'). Utilization % = balance at statement close ÷ credit limit × 100. Goal: under 30% per card, ideally under 10%.
example:
Jordan has a $5,000-limit credit card. Statement closes the 15th of each month. Payment due the 10th of the following month (~25-day grace).

Scenario A (most people):
  Sep 14: charge $4,500 (vacation, work expense, whatever)
  Sep 15: statement closes at $4,500 balance
  → Card issuer reports 90% utilization to bureaus
  Oct 10: Jordan pays the $4,500 in full ✓ (no interest)
  → But the credit score already took a hit from the 90% utilization report

Scenario B (the optimization):
  Sep 14: charge $4,500
  Sep 14 (same day): pay $4,000 of the charge
  Sep 15: statement closes at $500 balance
  → Card issuer reports 10% utilization
  Oct 10: Jordan pays the remaining $500 ✓
  → No interest AND a clean utilization report

Same total spending, same total paid, same total interest ($0). But B's credit score stays healthy while A's takes a temporary 20-40 point dip from the high utilization report.

A reminder: the grace period (per CARD Act / Reg Z) only protects new purchases. If you carry a prior-month balance, interest accrues from the transaction date.
realWorldHint: Use this to time your payment so it actually lowers your interest.

title: Pay off debt faster: avalanche vs snowball
concept: Avalanche: pay minimums on all debts, throw extra money at the highest-interest one first. Saves the most money mathematically. Snowball: pay minimums on all, throw extra at the smallest balance first. Gives quicker psychological wins. Avalanche always wins on math; snowball often wins on behavior.
shortcut: Avalanche: target the highest APR first. Snowball: target the smallest balance first. Interest saved by putting $X extra against the higher rate vs lower rate: $X × (highRate − lowRate) ÷ 12 per month. The difference between avalanche and snowball over time = your 'psychology premium.'
example:
Debt A: $5k at 24% APR
Debt B: $2k at 18% APR
