Avalanche: pay extra on A → saves more interest
$200 extra: $200 × (24% − 18%) ÷ 12 = $1/month saved
× 24 months = $24 psychology premium

Snowball pays off B first (motivating!), then A.
realWorldHint: Use this when you have multiple debts and need a payoff order.

title: APR — what it actually costs
concept: APR (Annual Percentage Rate) is the simple annual rate banks quote on every loan, credit card, BNPL agreement, and mortgage. By federal law (Truth in Lending Act / Reg Z, per CFPB), APR must include the interest rate plus most fees expressed as an annual rate — making it the standard comparison number across lenders. For installment loans (mortgage, auto, personal), the quoted APR captures your full cost. For revolving credit (cards), APR understates slightly because monthly compounding produces an effective rate ~5-10% higher than the headline APR — the 'APY' number that banks don't post on debt. (See `investing_apy_savings` for the APY version, used on savings.)
shortcut: Per-period rate = APR ÷ periods/year. Monthly rate on debt = APR ÷ 12. Monthly interest charge ≈ balance × APR ÷ 12. Annual interest cost (no compounding) = balance × APR. For revolving debt, real annual cost is slightly higher due to monthly compounding — but APR is the right comparison number across loans because it's standardized (per Reg Z).
example:
$5,000 balance on a 24% APR credit card:
Monthly rate: 24% ÷ 12 = 2%
Monthly interest charge: $100
Annual interest (simple): $1,200
Annual interest (with monthly compounding): ~$1,344
The ~$144 gap is the 'APR vs APY' difference banks don't highlight on debt.

Comparing two personal loan offers:
Loan A: 9.5% APR, no fees
Loan B: 8.5% rate, 2% origination fee → APR ≈ 9.7%
Loan A is the better deal — APR captures it correctly.
realWorldHint: Use this to understand the real rate a lender is quoting you.

title: Buy Now, Pay Later — the math they don't show
concept: BNPL splits a purchase into 4 'easy payments.' Sounds free. Miss one payment = up to $35 late fee (sometimes 25% of the missed payment). On a $300 purchase that's an 11.7% surcharge — higher than most credit card APRs. The real danger is stacking: CFPB market studies found heavy BNPL users juggling many loans at once and overdrafting their bank accounts at roughly twice the rate of non-users. Visibility is messy in BOTH directions: the plans don't show on your credit card statement (the cash drain is invisible to you), and whether they show on your credit REPORT depends on the provider — as of mid-2026, Affirm reports most of its loans to bureaus, while Klarna's and Afterpay's pay-in-4 plans generally aren't reported. But a missed plan sent to collections absolutely IS reported, and FICO has announced BNPL-aware score models — so assume visibility is rising, not falling.
shortcut: Total BNPL = number of payments × payment amount. Surcharge from one late fee = lateFee ÷ originalPrice × 100. Stacked monthly burden = sum of all your BNPL payments across providers. The clean test: if you can't pay cash today, you can't afford it.
example:
$300 item, 4 × $75 BNPL:
Miss one: $35 late fee
Total paid: $335
Surcharge: 11.7%

Typical user (per CFPB):
~9 BNPL loans/year stacked across Affirm/Klarna/Afterpay
Monthly burden invisible to credit reports
2× more likely to overdraft than non-users
realWorldHint: Remember this the next time 'pay in 4' pops up at checkout.

title: How credit scores actually work
concept: Most adults don't know what actually goes into their FICO score. The factors and weights: payment history (35%), credit utilization (30%), length of credit history (15%), credit mix (10%), recent inquiries (10%). What helps: paying on time, keeping utilization under 30%, having older accounts open. What hurts: late payments, high utilization, closing your oldest card. What doesn't matter: checking your own score, your income, your savings balance.
shortcut: Two things drive 65% of your score: pay on time, keep utilization low. That's it. The rest is minor. Most 'credit hacks' are noise compared to those two basics. Checking your own score is harmless. Closing old cards is harmful.
example:
FICO score factors:
Payment history     35%
Utilization         30%
Age of credit       15%
Credit mix          10%
New inquiries       10%

Utilization sweet spot: under 30%, ideally under 10%. On a $10k limit, keep balance under $3,000 (preferably under $1,000) at statement close.
realWorldHint: Use this before a big application to understand what moves your score.

title: Debt isn't 'good' or 'bad' — it's risk × cost
concept: The 'good debt vs bad debt' label is a moral framing that obscures the actual decision. A better mental model: every debt has two dimensions worth pricing — **cost** (interest rate, fees, opportunity cost of the payment) and **risk** (what happens if your income drops). Evaluate any debt on four factors that combine to score both axes: (1) **Rate** drives cost — under 6% is cheap, 6-10% is neutral, 10%+ is expensive in real terms. (2) **Asset** drives whether the cost is offset — appreciating (home, education) or depreciating (car, vacation). (3) **Cash flow** drives risk — does the monthly payment leave room in your budget if your income dips, or are you maxed out? (4) **Tax treatment** drives effective cost — mortgage interest and student-loan interest (up to AGI limits per IRS) are deductible; consumer debt isn't. A 3% mortgage on a 10-year-hold home scores low cost + offset asset + manageable cash flow + tax break: low cost, low risk. A 24% credit card on a vacation scores high cost + depreciating asset + likely cash-flow strain + no tax break: high cost, high risk. The exercise isn't to label debt good/bad — it's to price the cost-risk tradeoff before signing.
shortcut: Don't label debt good or bad — score two axes: cost (the rate; 10%+ is expensive) and risk (asset value, budget strain). High on both is almost always wrong; low on both is fine.
example:
$5,000 extra cash. Two pricings on the cost-risk grid:

(A) Pay off 22% APR credit card balance:
  Cost: HIGH — 22% rate, no tax deduction → real cost 22%
  Risk: HIGH — depreciating asset (already-spent dollars), strains DTI if balance is non-trivial
  Verdict: knock it out. 22% guaranteed return beats the ~10% expected return on an index fund. The behavioral premium (eliminating the variable monthly minimum) is on top.

(B) Prepay 3% mortgage instead:
  Cost: LOW — 3% rate, mortgage interest deductible at ~22% bracket → effective cost ~2.3%
  Risk: LOW — appreciating asset, manageable monthly
  Verdict: don't rush to prepay. Investing $5K at expected ~10% net of inflation beats saving 2.3% in interest by ~7 percentage points/year. The mortgage is a tool, not a problem.

Same $5K, opposite decisions — driven by the cost-risk grid, not by labeling either debt 'good' or 'bad.'
realWorldHint: Use this when you're deciding whether a debt is worth taking on.

title: Emergency fund vs debt payoff — what to do first
concept: One of the most common r/personalfinance questions: should your next $500 go toward an emergency fund or paying off debt? The widely-followed 'Order of Operations' (popularized by the r/personalfinance wiki and Dave Ramsey's baby steps): (1) build a $1,000 starter emergency fund first — enough to survive a small crisis without taking on new high-interest debt; (2) get any 401(k) employer match (instant ~50-100% return on contribution); (3) pay off high-interest debt (>~8% APR — typically credit cards, personal loans, payday loans); (4) build a fuller 3-6 month emergency fund of essentials; (5) max retirement and other long-term investing. The logic: a tiny EF stops the debt bleed before it restarts, the match is free money, and high-interest debt is a guaranteed loss bigger than any plausible investment gain.
shortcut: Order: $1k starter EF → 401k match → high-interest debt → full 3-6mo EF → max retirement. But build the tiny EF first if it stops you running up new debt every emergency.
example:
Three users with the same $500 extra cash:

(A) No EF, $4k credit card debt at 24% APR
→ Build $1k starter EF first, then attack the 24% debt. 24% guaranteed return beats any investment.

(B) $1k EF, no debt, employer offers 50% 401k match
→ Capture the match — it's a 50% instant return.

(C) $5k EF, no high-interest debt, $200k mortgage at 3.5%
→ Invest the $500. 3.5% mortgage is below long-run stock returns; don't rush to pay it off.
realWorldHint: Use this when you have spare cash and can't decide: save it or kill debt?

title: Rent affordability (28% rule)
concept: The 28% rule says your rent shouldn't exceed 28% of your gross monthly income. It's a quick gut check when apartment shopping — if a place costs more than 28% of what you earn before taxes, it's going to squeeze your budget.
shortcut: Max rent = monthly gross × 0.28. Reverse: min income for a given rent = rent ÷ 0.28. For $5,000/month: max rent = $1,400. For $2,000 rent: need $7,143/month gross = $85,714/year.
example:
Monthly salary: $5,000
Max rent: $5,000 × 28% = $1,400
realWorldHint: Use this before you start apartment hunting or sign a lease.

title: How much house can I afford?
concept: 'How much house can I afford?' is the single highest-volume personal-finance search query (~1M+/month on 'mortgage calculator' alone, per industry SEO tools). The honest answer involves 6+ variables: gross income, mortgage rate, down payment, property taxes, homeowner's insurance, and PMI (if down < 20%). The standard 28/36 rule (per Fannie Mae underwriting): max housing PITI ≤ 28% of GROSS monthly income; total debt service ≤ 36%. Once you know your max PITI, you back into the loan amount using the mortgage rate factor (~0.006 per $1 of loan at 6%/30yr), and add the down payment to get the max purchase price.
shortcut: Three steps: (1) Max PITI = gross monthly × 0.28. (2) After subtracting est. tax + insurance (rough rule: ~1.5%/yr of price ÷ 12), what's left is your max P&I. (3) Max loan = P&I ÷ rate factor (0.006 at 6%, 0.0054 at 5%, 0.0067 at 7%). Add down payment to get max purchase price. PMI adds ~0.5%/yr to the loan if down < 20% — bake that into your tax/insurance estimate.
example:
$7,000/mo gross income, 6.5% rate (factor ~0.00632), 10% down:
Max PITI = $7,000 × 28% = $1,960
Est. tax+ins on a $300k home: 1.5% × $300k ÷ 12 = $375/mo (assume $300k as starting estimate)
Max P&I = $1,960 − $375 = $1,585
Max loan ≈ $1,585 ÷ 0.00632 ≈ $251,000
Max purchase price = $251k loan + $28k (10% down) ≈ $279k
(Below 20% down, add ~0.5% PMI: ~$105/mo, reducing the loan headroom slightly.)
realWorldHint: Use this before you talk to a lender or tour your first home.

title: Cash to close — the number that surprises first-time buyers
concept: The purchase price of a home is NOT the cash you need at the closing table. A first-time buyer typically needs the down payment PLUS another **2-5% of the purchase price in closing costs** (per CFPB Consumer Closing Costs research) — loan origination, title insurance, appraisal, inspection, recording fees, prepaid escrow for property tax + insurance, prepaid interest from closing date to month-end, and (if down < 20%) the first PMI premium. Lender requirements typically include 2-3 months of mortgage reserves on top of all this. Then add the moves-related cash that doesn't show on the settlement statement: moving truck ($300-3,000), utility setup deposits ($200-500), and immediate household setup costs that the new home requires. The honest mental shortcut: **cash to close ≈ down payment + 5% of purchase price + ~$2-3K for moving**. On a $400K home with 10% down, that's $40K down + ~$20K closing/escrow + ~$3K moving = roughly **$63K in cash needed before keys**, not the $40K most buyers budget.
shortcut: Cash to close ≈ down payment + 5% of purchase price (covers closing costs, escrow, reserves) + ~$2-3K moving/setup. For a quick screening rule: if you're putting 10% down, plan to have 15% of the purchase price in liquid cash before signing the offer. If you're putting 20% down, plan for 25%. Anything less and you're either rolling closing costs into the loan (extra interest) or scrambling for cash at the last minute (deals fall through this way).
example:
Realistic cash-to-close on a $400,000 home, 10% down, 6.5% rate, first-time buyer:

Down payment (10%):              $40,000
Loan origination + lender fees:   $4,000  (1% of $360K loan)
Title insurance + escrow + recording: $3,500
Appraisal + inspection:           $1,000
Prepaid property tax + insurance (escrow): $4,500  (2 months of est. $375 tax+ins × 6 months)
Prepaid interest (closing date to end of month): $1,200
First PMI premium (10% down):     $150
Lender-required cash reserves (2 months PITI verified): doesn't leave account, but must be visible
────────────────
Cash at closing table:           $54,350

Plus moving / setup:
  Moving truck or movers:        $1,500
  Utility deposits:              $400
  Immediate household setup (appliances, basic furniture, light fixtures): $3,500
────────────────
Total cash before move-in:       ~$59,750

Quick mental shortcut applied: $40K + 5% × $400K + $3K moving = $40K + $20K + $3K = $63K. Within $4K of the line-item answer.

The $20K gap between 'down payment = $40K' (what most buyers anchor on) and 'cash to close = $60K' is the single largest first-time-buyer surprise. Save for the whole number, not the down payment alone.
realWorldHint: Run this before closing day so the cash you need doesn't blindside you.

title: Cost-of-living move — is your $15K raise still a raise?
concept: A job offer with a higher salary in a higher-cost city often nets out to less real income than your current job. Three components of a real-income comparison: (1) **Salary delta** — the headline raise. (2) **Housing delta** — typical year-over-year rent gap between cities is the largest single line. SF / NYC / Boston / LA / Seattle / DC rent $2,500-3,500 for a 1BR vs $1,200-1,800 in Austin / Denver / Raleigh / Phoenix (per Apartment List + Zumper city rent reports). On a 12-month basis, a $1,000/mo rent jump erases $12,000 of a $15,000 raise before any tax change. (3) **Tax delta** — state income tax varies from 0% (TX / FL / WA / NV) to 6-13% (CA / NY / NJ / HI). A $90K salary moving from Austin (0% state) to NYC (~6% state + 3% city) loses ~$8,100/year in additional income tax. Real-income mental shortcut: **real change = annual salary delta − annual rent delta − annual tax delta**. Anything else (commute cost, sales tax, COL on groceries) matters at the margins but housing + state tax are 80% of the gap.
shortcut: Real raise = nominal raise − (rent delta × 12) − (state tax % delta × new salary). If the new city raises rent $600/mo, that's $7,200 of your raise gone before taxes. If you're also moving from no-state-tax (TX/FL) to high-state-tax (CA/NY), subtract another 5-10% of the new salary. Net positive moves are common; net negative moves (a 'raise' that's a real pay cut) are also common — running the 3-number subtraction saves bad decisions.
example:
Two real moves with the 3-number subtraction:

Case A — Austin → SF, $25K raise:
  Current Austin: $95K salary, 0% state tax, $1,800/mo rent
  Offer SF: $120K salary, 9.3% effective CA tax, $3,500/mo rent

  Salary delta: +$25,000
  Rent delta: ($3,500 − $1,800) × 12 = −$20,400
  Tax delta: (9.3% − 0%) × $120K = −$11,160
  Real change: +$25K − $20.4K − $11.2K = **−$6,600/year** (the 'raise' is actually a $6K REAL pay cut)

Case B — Austin → Raleigh, $15K raise:
  Current Austin: $95K, 0% state tax, $1,800 rent
  Offer Raleigh: $110K, ~5% NC state tax, $1,500 rent

  Salary delta: +$15,000
  Rent delta: ($1,500 − $1,800) × 12 = +$3,600 (rent goes DOWN)
  Tax delta: (5% − 0%) × $110K = −$5,500
  Real change: +$15K + $3.6K − $5.5K = **+$13,100/year** (real raise, almost the full headline)

Same nominal $15-25K 'raise,' wildly different real outcomes. Always run the 3 subtractions before accepting the offer.
realWorldHint: Use this when a job in a new city offers more money.

title: First-month true cost — what it really takes to move in
concept: Existing lesson 6.4 (move-in cost) covers the rent-component cash: first + last + security deposit + broker. Reality is bigger. A complete first-month-in-a-new-place includes: (1) the rent-component cash (typically 3-4× monthly rent before keys). (2) **Utility setup** — electricity / gas deposits ($100-300 if no credit history, sometimes refundable), internet activation ($100-200 with installation), water/sewer setup. (3) **Furniture and setup** — even with most of your stuff coming with you, expect $500-3,000 in unavoidable additions (mattress if no fit, curtains, kitchen basics, shower curtain, garbage cans, cleaning supplies). (4) **Moving** — $300-700 (truck rental only, you do the labor) up to $2,000-4,000 (movers, including packing). (5) **Grocery restock** — $200-500 to refill from empty pantry/fridge/spices. (6) **Renters insurance** — $10-20/month, typically paid annually $120-240 upfront. The first-month total typically lands 5-7× monthly rent — much higher than the 3-4× rent-only move-in calc suggests.
shortcut: First-month true cost ≈ rent move-in cash + ~$3-4K of utilities/furniture/moving/restock for a typical 1BR move. For budget planning: pad the rent-only move-in number by **$3,000 base + 1,000 per bedroom**. So a 1BR is move-in cost + $4,000; a 2BR shared is move-in cost + $5,000. Half of these add-ons (utility deposits, renters insurance) are refundable or pre-paid for future months — but the cash still has to clear up front.
example:
Sam moves from a furnished sublet into a $1,800/mo 1BR apartment in a no-broker city.

Rent-component cash (first + last + security):
  First month: $1,800
  Last month: $1,800
  Security deposit: $1,800
  Subtotal: $5,400

Add-ons most people forget:
  Electricity activation deposit (no rental history): $150
  Internet installation + first month: $250
  Renters insurance (annual): $180
  Movers (small 1BR, local): $700
  Mattress (sublet had one, new place doesn't): $600
  Kitchen basics + cleaning + shower curtain + light bulbs: $400
  Grocery restock (empty pantry, spices, oils, condiments): $300
  Subtotal: $2,580

First-month TRUE cost: $5,400 + $2,580 = **$7,980**

Vs the headline 'move-in cost' from lesson 6.4 of $5,400 — the gap is $2,580 or about 48%. The quick add-on shortcut ($3,000 base + $1,000/bedroom = $4,000 padding) lands $1,400 high here, but errs on the safe side, which is the right direction for cash-flow planning.

What to skip: avoid signing up for non-essential 'apartment setup' services and bundled internet/cable packages on day one — wait two weeks to see what you actually need.
realWorldHint: Run this before you move so the upfront cash doesn't catch you off guard.

title: Rent increase math
concept: When your landlord raises rent by a percentage, the dollar impact depends on your current rent. National average increase is 3-5% — anything above 5% is aggressive. The renewal-vs-move decision often comes down to: how many months of higher rent equals the cost of moving?
shortcut: Increase $ = rent × increase%. Compare to 4% average to spot aggressive hikes. Renewal-vs-move: moving cost ÷ monthly increase = months until staying costs more.
example:
$1,500 rent, 7% increase:
$105 more/mo, $1,260/yr
7% vs avg 4% = aggressive

Move costs $4,200, increase $120/mo:
Break-even: $4,200 ÷ $120 = 35 months
If lease is 12 months, staying is cheaper.
realWorldHint: Use this when your renewal letter arrives with a higher number.

title: Move-in cost calculator
concept: Moving into a new place often requires first month's rent, last month's rent, and a security deposit upfront. Some cities add broker fees. The total can be 3–4× your monthly rent, which catches people off guard.
shortcut: Move-in = first + last + deposit (+ broker fee). For $1,800/month with a broker fee equal to one month's rent: $1,800 × 4 = $7,200 due before you get the keys.
example:
Rent: $1,800/month
First + last + deposit + broker
$1,800 × 4 = $7,200 move-in
realWorldHint: Run this before you sign so you know the full upfront cost.

title: The roommate math — $6,500/year
concept: A roommate is the single biggest housing decision for renters. Studies of rent-vs-1BR-vs-shared-2BR across major US cities (e.g. Apartment List, Zumper, RentCafe annual rental reports) consistently find a ~$500-700/month savings — roughly $6,000-$8,500/year — from sharing a 2BR vs renting a 1BR solo, before utilities and household supplies (which also split). In the highest-rent cities (SF, NYC, Boston), the savings can hit 40-50%.
shortcut: Annual saving = (1BR + 1BR utilities) − (shared 2BR + 2BR utilities) / 2. Unequal split? Bigger bedroom = 55%, smaller = 45%. Most apartment splits should be slightly uneven based on room size.
example:
1BR alone: $1,800 rent + $200 util = $2,000/mo
2BR shared: $2,400 rent + $250 util
Your half: $1,325/mo
Savings: $675/mo, $8,100/yr

Unequal split (bigger room):
2BR $2,400 × 55% = $1,320 for you
realWorldHint: Use this when deciding whether a roommate is worth the trade-offs.

title: What renting actually costs you each month
concept: Rent is the headline number, not the actual cost. The true monthly housing cost = rent + renter's insurance + utilities + parking + laundry + commute. Typically 15-25% more than rent alone. The 28% rule should be applied to TOTAL housing cost, not just rent.
shortcut: Add all housing-adjacent monthly bills. That's your real monthly housing cost. Quick add-on rule: rent × 1.20 ≈ true cost for most renters. Apply 28% rule to THAT, not the rent alone.
example:
Rent: $1,500
Insurance: $15
Utilities: $150
Parking: $100
Laundry: $40
True cost: $1,805/mo (+20%)

Income $5,500: 28% cap = $1,540
Apartment 'fits' at rent — fails on true cost.
realWorldHint: Use this to see what renting really costs you beyond the rent line.

title: Mortgage payment, the right way
concept: Mental-math mortgage estimates: at 5% over 30 years, payment ≈ loan × 0.00537. At 6%, × 0.006. At 7%, × 0.00665. These factors come from actual amortization — they're accurate within $5 on typical loans. Old shortcut (interest + principal portions) overestimates by ~30%.
shortcut: At 6% over 30 yrs: monthly ≈ loan × 0.006. At 5%: × 0.0054. At 7%: × 0.0067. Per $100k borrowed at 6%: $600/mo. $300k loan? $1,800/mo. Add ~$300 for property tax + insurance.
example:
$300,000 mortgage at 6%, 30 years:
$300k × 0.006 = $1,800/mo
Actual amortized: $1,799 ✓

Vs renting $1,900?
P&I cheaper by $100
+ tax/insurance ~$300 = $2,100
Rent slightly cheaper
realWorldHint: Use this to estimate a real mortgage payment before you shop.

title: Should I break my lease? The math
concept: Early termination fees average 2-4 months' rent. Add moving costs ($1,200-$2,500). Compare to: how much you'd save monthly at the new place × remaining months on lease. If break cost > near-term savings, stay.
shortcut: Total break cost = months penalty × rent + moving cost. Break-even = break cost ÷ monthly saving. If lease has fewer months left than break-even, staying is cheaper.
example:
Lease: 8 months left at $1,800
Break fee: 2 months = $3,600
Moving: $1,200
Total break cost: $4,800

New apartment: $1,500/mo ($300 saving)
Break-even: $4,800 ÷ $300 = 16 months
Only 8 left → STAY, save $2,400
realWorldHint: Run this when you're deciding whether to break your lease early.

title: Buy vs rent — the real decision framework
concept: The buy-vs-rent decision depends on three things in this order: (1) **Timeline** — under 5 years almost always favors renting because closing costs (2-5% buying + 6% selling = ~8-11% round-trip) typically exceed any equity gained. (2) **Mortgage rate** — the old 'rent × 200 = purchase price' rule worked at 3-4% rates; in a 7% rate environment, you need to compare actual monthly PITI to rent, not a flat multiplier. (3) **Opportunity cost** — your down payment could be invested instead. $60k down vs $60k in an index fund at 10% ≈ $156k after 10 years.
shortcut: Staying under 5 years? Rent. Otherwise compare monthly PITI to rent — at today's ~7% rates, buying usually pencils out only when rent × 150–180 stays under the purchase price.
example:
Rate-sensitive multiplier:
3-4% mortgage era: rent × 200 ≈ break-even purchase price
6-7% mortgage era: rent × 150-180 ≈ break-even

At $2,000/mo rent:
  4% rates: buying ≤$400k makes sense
  7% rates: buying ≤$300-360k makes sense
  Above those, renting + investing the difference often wins

Job stability test:
Might move in 2 years? → Rent
Committed to city 10+ years? → Buy (after running the math)
realWorldHint: Use this when everyone insists renting is 'throwing money away.'

title: What's in a lease — clauses that matter
concept: Most renters sign leases without reading them. The clauses that bite later: subletting (often prohibited), early termination penalties (typically 2 months rent), automatic renewal (you may be locked in 60-90 days before lease ends), security deposit return timelines (varies by state — most require 14-30 days), and what counts as 'damage' vs 'normal wear and tear'.
shortcut: Three things to check before signing: (1) early termination penalty (2 months max is reasonable; 4+ is predatory), (2) auto-renewal clause and notice period, (3) what the security deposit can be deducted for. Negotiate before signing — landlords rarely re-open after.
example:
Common predatory clauses:
— Auto-renewal with 90-day notice (you forget, locked in another year)
— Sublet forbidden under any condition (no flexibility)
— Security deposit non-refundable in certain conditions (illegal in most states)
— 'Tenant responsible for all repairs' (illegal in most states)

Know your state's tenant rights. Many cities offer free tenant advisory services.
realWorldHint: Read this before you sign any lease.

title: Marginal tax brackets
concept: Two things most people get wrong about federal tax brackets. (1) Brackets apply to TAXABLE income, not gross. Taxable income = gross − standard deduction (or itemized) − any above-the-line deductions. The 2026 single standard deduction is $16,100 (per IRS Rev Proc 2025-32). (2) Brackets are marginal layers, not flat rates. 'Being in the 22% bracket' means only your dollars ABOVE $50,400 are taxed at 22% — the first $12,400 is taxed at 10%, the next slice up to $50,400 is taxed at 12%. So your effective rate is always lower than your top bracket.
shortcut: Two-step mental: (1) Taxable income = gross − $16,100 standard deduction (single, 2026). (2) Stack the slices: first $12,400 at 10%, next slice up to $50,400 at 12%, next slice up to $105,700 at 22%. Then add. For a quick sanity check, your effective rate on a $60K gross income single filer lands around 8–11% — well below the headline 22% bracket.
realWorldHint: Use this to estimate what you actually owe — and stop fearing a higher bracket.

title: Paycheck deductions
concept: Your gross pay gets reduced by FICA (6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare = 7.65% combined), federal income tax, and state income tax before you see a dime. Two FICA nuances for higher earners: Social Security applies only up to the annual wage base (~$184,500 for 2026 per SSA) — above that, only the 1.45% Medicare portion continues. Workers earning over $200k single / $250k MFJ also pay the Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% on income above that threshold (per IRS).
shortcut: Net pay = gross × (1 − total deduction rate). If FICA is 7.65%, federal is 12%, and state is 5%, total rate = 24.65%. From $4,000 gross: $4,000 × 0.7535 = $3,014 net. Earning above the SS wage base? Knock the rate down by 6.2% on dollars above the cap.
example:
Gross: $4,000/mo (~$48k/yr, below SS cap)
FICA (7.65%): $306
Federal (12%): $480
State (5%): $200
Net: $3,014

High earner above $184,500 (2026):
On dollars above the cap, only 1.45% Medicare applies (plus 0.9% Additional Medicare above $200k single).
realWorldHint: Use this to decode why your paycheck is smaller than your salary.

title: Your tax refund is not a bonus
concept: A $3,000 refund means you gave the government a $250/month interest-free loan all year. That's not a windfall — it's your own money returned without interest. If you'd adjusted your W-4 and invested $250/month at 6% instead, you'd have ~$3,100 by year-end — more than the refund.
shortcut: Refund ÷ pay periods = how much extra you should have kept per paycheck. Refund × ~3% = roughly what you forfeited in lost growth over the year. Big refund = poorly-set W-4, not a bonus.
example:
Refund: $3,000
Monthly over-withholding: $250

If invested at 6%/yr:
~$3,100 at year-end
Extra ~$100 vs lump refund

Over 10 years of same pattern:
Forfeited >$1,000 in compounding
realWorldHint: Remember this when a big refund feels like a win.

title: Self-employment tax
concept: Freelancers and gig workers pay both halves of FICA (15.3% nominal) plus regular income tax. IRS Schedule SE applies the 15.3% to 92.35% of net SE earnings (you deduct the employer-equivalent half first), so the effective SE rate is ~14.13%. There's no employer withholding, so the IRS requires quarterly estimated payments (April, June, Sept, Jan). Skip them and pay a penalty. The 'set aside' rate varies by state: 30% covers most people in no-income-tax states (TX, FL, WA, NV); add 5-10% in high-tax states (CA, NY, NJ). When in doubt, set aside 35% — easier to refund yourself than scramble at tax time.
shortcut: Effective SE tax ≈ income × 14.13% (15.3% applied to 92.35% of earnings). Set aside per state: TX/FL/WA/NV → 30%. Most states → 32-33%. CA/NY/NJ/HI → 35-40%. Quarterly estimated payment = (income × 14.13%) + (income × income-tax rate). Better to over-save and refund yourself than under-save and panic in April.
example:
$5,000 freelance income:
SE tax: $5,000 × 92.35% × 15.3% = $707
+ federal income tax ~15-20%
+ state income tax ~0-13%

Total set-aside guidance:
TX/FL (no state tax): ~30% = $1,500
Most states: ~33% = $1,650
CA/NY: ~37% = $1,850

Quarterly:
$8,000/quarter at ~30% combined
= ~$2,400 estimated payment due
realWorldHint: Run this if you freelance, so quarterly taxes don't wreck you.

title: Standard vs itemized — which saves you more?
concept: The 2026 standard deduction is $16,100 single / $24,150 Head of Household / $32,200 married filing jointly. Itemize only if mortgage interest + state/local taxes (the SALT deduction cap rose to $40,400 in 2026 under OBBBA, phasing down for incomes above $500K MAGI) + charity beats your filing status's standard. After the 2017 tax law (made permanent by OBBBA in 2025), ~90% of filers take the standard. Homeowners with mortgages and high-tax-state residents (NY, CA, NJ) are the main itemizers.
shortcut: Add mortgage interest + state taxes + charity. If > $16,100 (single), $24,150 (HoH), or $32,200 (MFJ) for your filing status, itemize. Extra tax saving vs standard = (itemized − standard) × your marginal tax rate.
example:
Single, 22% tax bracket:
Mortgage interest: $10,500
State taxes: $5,100
Charity: $1,800
Itemized: $17,400
Standard (single): $16,100
Extra saving: $1,300 × 22% ≈ $286

Head of Household same numbers? Standard = $24,150 — itemizing loses by ~$6,750; take the standard.
realWorldHint: Use this at tax time to pick the deduction that saves you more.

title: Sell too soon, pay double the tax
concept: Short-term capital gains (held < 1 year) are taxed at your ordinary income rate (22-24% for most). Long-term gains (held > 1 year) are taxed at 0%, 15%, or 20% (for 2026, single filers stay in the 15% rate up to $545,500 of taxable income, per IRS Rev Proc 2025-32). High earners also owe the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax (NIIT) on investment gains once MAGI tops $200K single / $250K MFJ (per IRC § 1411). For most of the target audience, the long-vs-short gap is ~7 percentage points. Waiting a few weeks past the 1-year mark can save thousands.
shortcut: On a $10k gain at 22% ordinary rate: short-term = $2,200 tax. Long-term at 15% = $1,500. Wait one extra month = save $700. Per $10k of gain, waiting saves ~$700.
example:
Held stock 11 months, $15k gain:
Sell now (short-term, 24%):
$15k × 24% = $3,600 tax

Wait 1 more month (long-term, 15%):
$15k × 15% = $2,250 tax
Save: $1,350
realWorldHint: Use this before you sell an investment you've held close to a year.

title: Stop lending the government your money
concept: Your W-4 determines how much tax is withheld per paycheck. If you consistently get a refund over $500, you're over-withholding — handing the government an interest-free loan. Reducing withholding by refund ÷ pay periods means more cash each paycheck that you can invest or save.
shortcut: Last year's refund ÷ pay periods = bump per paycheck. $3,000 refund ÷ 26 biweekly = $115/check extra. Invested at 6%/year, that compounds to slightly MORE than the refund within a year.
example:
Refund: $3,000
Biweekly paychecks: 26
Per-paycheck bump: $115

Invest $115/check at 6%:
Year-end value: ~$3,100
Vs lump refund $3,000
Gain: ~$100 + control of cash
realWorldHint: Use this when you keep getting big refunds and want that cash sooner.

title: Your paycheck stub + filing status
concept: Two things on every US worker's paycheck most never decode: (1) the **stub line items** (gross pay, FICA at 7.65%, federal/state withholding, pre-tax vs post-tax deductions), and (2) the **filing status** used to compute withholding — Single, Married Filing Jointly (MFJ), Married Filing Separately (MFS), Head of Household (HoH), or Qualifying Widow(er). Filing status drives your bracket, standard deduction, and credit eligibility. Two important nuances: 401(k) contributions reduce income tax but NOT FICA; HSA contributions via Section 125 reduce BOTH (extra ~7.65% advantage per IRS Pub 15-B). And single parents providing >50% of household costs are usually HoH not Single — bigger standard deduction.
shortcut: 401(k) cuts income tax but still pays FICA; HSA/Section 125 premiums cut both. Filing status defaults to Single, but jump to Head of Household if you cover >50% of a household.
example:
Sample biweekly stub on $80k MFJ filer:
Gross pay        $3,077
— Pre-tax 401k    −$308 (10%)
— Pre-tax HSA     −$150 (via Sec 125)
  Income-taxable  $2,619
  FICA-taxable    $2,769  (401k still pays FICA; HSA doesn't)
— Federal tax     −$315 (MFJ brackets)
— State tax       −$133
— FICA (7.65%)    −$212
  Net pay         $2,000

Standard deduction 2026 by status:
  Single: $16,100  ·  HoH: $24,150  ·  MFJ: $32,200
Picking the wrong status can cost a single parent $8,050 in extra taxable income (Single vs HoH).
realWorldHint: Use this to actually read your pay stub and pick the right filing status.

title: Deductible vs premium tradeoff
concept: Your premium is the floor — what you pay every month no matter what. Your deductible adds to your ceiling — the worst-case annual exposure if something major happens. Higher deductible = lower floor but higher ceiling. This is the simplified model; lessons 2-3 add coinsurance and the OOP cap.
shortcut: Floor (best-case annual) = premium × 12. Ceiling (simplified worst-case) = floor + deductible. Range = deductible. That range is your financial exposure if you have a bad year.
example:
Plan A: $350/mo, $1,000 deductible
Floor: $4,200/year (healthy year)
Ceiling: $5,200 (full deductible spent)
Exposure: $1,000

Plan B: $250/mo, $3,000 deductible
Floor: $3,000
Ceiling: $6,000
Exposure: $3,000
realWorldHint: Use this when picking a health plan during open enrollment.

title: Copay vs coinsurance
concept: A copay is a flat fee per visit ($30 per doctor visit). Coinsurance is a percentage of the bill you pay after the deductible is met (you pay 20%, insurance pays 80%). On expensive procedures, coinsurance adds up fast — 20% of a $10,000 surgery is $2,000.
shortcut: Your coinsurance cost = total bill × your coinsurance %. On a $5,000 bill with 20% coinsurance: $5,000 × 20% = $1,000 out of your pocket.
example:
Surgery: $8,000
Deductible already met
Coinsurance: 20%
You pay: $8,000 × 20% = $1,600
Insurance pays: $6,400
realWorldHint: Use this to predict what a doctor visit or procedure will cost you.

title: Out-of-pocket maximum
concept: The out-of-pocket max caps what you pay for COVERED, IN-NETWORK care in a plan year. Once you hit it (deductible + coinsurance + qualifying copays), the plan pays 100% the rest of the year. It does NOT include your monthly premiums, out-of-network balance billing, or services your plan doesn't cover at all. So 'OOP max' is your worst case within the plan's rules — not necessarily your worst total spend if something falls outside them.
shortcut: After deductible, pay coinsurance until you hit the OOP max. On a $50,000 in-network hospital stay with $2,000 deductible and $6,000 OOP max: you pay at most $6,000 for that care; insurance covers the rest. Add 12 × premium to get your real annual outlay in a max-use year.
example:
In-network hospital bill: $50,000
Deductible: $2,000
Coinsurance: 20%
OOP max: $6,000
You pay for that care: $6,000 (capped)
Insurance: $44,000

Not counted: premiums ($300/mo × 12 = $3,600), any out-of-network charges, non-covered services.
realWorldHint: Use this to know the most a bad health year can cost you.

title: HDHP vs PPO comparison
concept: A High-Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) has lower premiums but higher deductibles. A PPO has higher premiums but lower out-of-pocket costs. HDHPs make sense if you're healthy and rarely use healthcare. PPOs win if you have regular medical needs or expect major procedures.
shortcut: HDHP total = lower premium × 12 + higher deductible. PPO total = higher premium × 12 + lower deductible. If HDHP worst-case < PPO worst-case, HDHP saves money. Also: HDHPs qualify for HSAs.
example:
HDHP: $200/mo, $3,000 deductible
Worst case: $5,400

PPO: $400/mo, $500 deductible
Worst case: $5,300

PPO wins by $100 in worst case
but HDHP saves $2,400 if healthy
realWorldHint: Use this when choosing between a high-deductible plan and a PPO.

title: HSA triple tax advantage
concept: HSAs have the triple tax advantage: contributions are pre-tax (reduce taxable income AND payroll tax if via Section 125), growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical are tax-free at any age. The hidden superpower: after age 65, you can withdraw HSA funds for ANY purpose (just pay ordinary income tax, like a Traditional IRA). 2026 contribution limits: $4,400 self-only / $8,750 family (per IRS Rev Proc 2025-19). You must be enrolled in a qualifying HDHP (2026 minimum deductible: $1,700 self / $3,400 family) to contribute. This combination makes the HSA arguably the most tax-efficient retirement account in the US code.
shortcut: Annual tax saving = contribution × (your income tax rate + ~7.65% FICA if contributed via payroll). Long-term: HSA grows like an investment account. $3,500/yr from age 30 to 65 at 7% growth ≈ $550,000, all tax-free for medical or income-taxed for anything else.
example:
Contribute $3,000 at 22% rate via payroll:
Income tax saved: $660
FICA saved (7.65%): $230
Total immediate saving: $890

Long-term:
$3,500/yr × 35 yrs at 7% growth
≈ $550,000
Used for medical: $0 tax
Used for retirement (after 65): ordinary income tax only
realWorldHint: Use this when you have an HDHP and aren't using the HSA's tax break.

title: FSA: free money or wasted money?
concept: Flexible Spending Accounts are use-it-or-lose-it: any unspent balance at year-end is generally forfeited. Employers can offer one (not both) of two grace mechanisms: a 2.5-month grace period to spend prior-year funds, or a limited rollover (IRS-indexed; ~$680 for 2026 per IRS Rev Proc 2025-32). 2026 contribution cap: $3,400 per employee (per IRS). Tax savings = election × your tax rate. If you elect $3,000 at a 25% bracket, you save $750 in tax. But if you only spend $1,800, you forfeit $1,200 — for a net loss of $450.
shortcut: Only elect what you'll definitely spend. Tax savings = election × tax rate. Break-even: spend at least (1 − tax rate) of your election. In a 25% bracket, you need to spend at least 75% of what you elect to come out ahead.
example:
Election: $2,850 at 25% bracket
Tax savings: $712

Scenario A: Spend $2,850 → save $712 ✓
Scenario B: Spend $1,800 → save $712 in tax but lose $1,050 unused
Net: −$338
realWorldHint: Run this before open enrollment so you don't over- or under-fund your FSA.

title: How much life insurance do you actually need?
concept: Two methods: (1) The 10-12× rule of thumb — multiply annual income by 10. (2) DIME method: Debt + Income replacement + Mortgage + Education costs. Add mortgage balance, subtract savings/existing coverage. Term life (20-30 years) is what most young families need — way cheaper than whole life.
shortcut: Quick estimate: salary × 10 = baseline coverage. Adjusted: + mortgage − savings. Compare two quotes by the annual cost per $100k of coverage.
example:
Salary: $70,000
10× rule: $700,000 baseline
Mortgage: +$280,000
Savings: −$50,000
Adjusted: $930,000 needed

Term quotes (30yr, healthy 35yo):
$500k @ $35/mo = $420/yr
$1M @ $55/mo = $660/yr
realWorldHint: Use this when someone depends on your income and you need coverage.

title: Brand name vs generic — the prescription math
concept: Generic drugs are chemically identical to brand-name versions but cost 80-85% less. With 12 monthly refills, a $35 copay difference becomes $420/year. When your doctor prescribes a brand-name drug, always ask if there's a generic.
shortcut: Annual saving per prescription = (brand copay − generic copay) × 12. For multiple prescriptions, sum the differences. Sometimes GoodRx cash price for generics is cheaper than insurance brand copay.
example:
Brand copay: $45
Generic copay: $10
Monthly diff: $35
Annual saving: $420

Two prescriptions switched to generic:
($35 + $20) × 12 = $660/year saved
realWorldHint: Use this at the pharmacy when there's a generic option.

title: What insurance policies do you actually need?
concept: Most adults are over-insured on some policies (extended warranties, pet insurance) and under-insured on others (disability, umbrella liability). The priority order: health > auto/renter's-or-home > life (with dependents) > disability > umbrella > pet > extended warranty. The principle: SELF-INSURE small risks (extended warranties, low deductibles), TRANSFER catastrophic ones (health, disability, liability).
shortcut: Rule: insure against what would be financially ruinous, NOT against minor inconveniences. A broken phone is annoying ($800). A hospital stay or year of disability is ruinous ($50k-$500k). Skip extended warranties, raise your auto deductible, but max out health and consider disability.
example:
Priority order (essential to optional):
1. Health insurance       — catastrophic protection
2. Auto + renter's/home   — required + liability
3. Life (if dependents)   — replace your income
4. Disability             — far more likely than death
5. Umbrella liability     — once net worth > $500k
6. Pet insurance          — optional
7. Extended warranties    — almost never worth it
realWorldHint: Use this to figure out which insurance you actually need — and which to skip.

title: Disability insurance — the one no one talks about
concept: You're statistically far more likely to be disabled than to die during your working years. The Social Security Administration estimates about 1 in 4 of today's 20-year-olds will become disabled before reaching retirement age (per SSA Disability Basic Facts). Yet most workers carry only basic employer-provided long-term disability — typically 60% of base salary, capped, and on an 'any-occupation' definition (no payout if you can do ANY job, even minimum-wage).
shortcut: On disability coverage, check own-occupation vs any-occupation, the coverage cap, and the elimination period — the ~90-day wait your emergency fund has to bridge.
example:
Why disability > life insurance for most working-age adults (per SSA):
Probability before age 65:
  Disability 90+ days: ~25%
  Death: ~5-7%

Employer LTD limits hurt high earners:
  Salary $200k, LTD pays 60% = $120k
  Capped at $10k/month = $120k/yr cap
  Above $200k earners may need supplemental private coverage.
realWorldHint: Use this to protect the paycheck everything else depends on.

title: Open enrollment — the 10-minute checklist
concept: Open enrollment is the ~2-week window each fall (typically Oct-Nov for a plan year starting Jan 1) when you pick all your employer benefits for the next 12 months. Miss it and you're locked in until next year unless you have a qualifying life event (marriage, baby, divorce, job loss). The mistake most people make: re-electing the same things from last year on autopilot. The 10-minute checklist that beats most people's outcomes: (1) **Medical plan** — HDHP vs PPO based on EXPECTED use this year (low: HDHP wins on premium; high: PPO wins on OOP). (2) **HSA or FSA** — HSA only if HDHP enrolled, $4,400 self / $8,750 family 2026 cap (per IRS Rev Proc 2025-19); FSA $3,400/yr 2026 cap (per IRS), use-it-or-lose-it. (3) **Dependent Care FSA** — $7,500/yr cap (raised from $5,000 by OBBBA 2025, the first increase since 1986; $3,750 if married filing separately), pre-tax for daycare / aftercare. (4) **Commuter benefits** — $340/mo each for transit + parking (2026, per IRS), pre-tax. (5) **Life insurance** — most employers give 1× salary free; supplemental usually 2-5× pre-tax. (6) **Disability** — confirm short-term and long-term coverage; check 'own-occupation' vs 'any-occupation' definitions. (7) **401(k) contribution rate** — open enrollment is also a good moment to bump.
shortcut: Estimate your medical year (low/medium/high), pick HDHP or PPO to match, then fund HSA with HDHP or FSA with PPO. DCFSA if you have kids, supplemental life only if you have dependents.
example:
Decision flow for a typical 30-something:

Single, healthy, no kids, low medical use:
  Medical: HDHP (lowest premium, low OOP risk)
  HSA: max out ($4,400 self, 2026) — triple tax advantage
  FSA: skip (HDHPs and Health FSAs don't combine; limited-purpose FSA allowed)
  DCFSA: skip (no dependents)
  Commuter: yes if commuting
  Supplemental life: skip (no dependents)
  Supplemental disability: maybe (cheap pre-tax via employer)
  Estimated annual tax saving: ~$1,200-1,800 from HSA alone at 22-24% bracket

Married with infant in daycare:
  Medical: PPO (kids = high medical-use risk)
  HSA: not available (PPO usually not HSA-eligible)
  FSA: $3,400 (2026) for predictable medical / dental / vision
  DCFSA: $7,500 (2026) for daycare — typically the highest-ROI election
  Commuter: yes
  Supplemental life: 2-5× salary (dependent income replacement)
  Estimated annual tax saving: ~$1,500-2,200 (FSA + DCFSA + commuter combined)

The 10-minute pass beats 90% of 'I just re-elected last year's plan' outcomes — most people leave $500-1,500/yr of tax savings on the table by skipping the DCFSA or commuter election.
realWorldHint: Use this during your ~2-week open enrollment window each fall.

title: Medical bill vs EOB — the number you actually owe
concept: Two documents arrive after any medical service that isn't a $30 copay: a **bill from the provider** and an **Explanation of Benefits (EOB) from your insurer**. They are not the same and they often disagree. The EOB shows what the provider billed, what insurance paid, what was 'adjusted off' via your insurer's negotiated rate, and what you OWE (the patient-responsibility line). The provider's bill should equal the EOB's patient-responsibility line — but research from Consumer Reports / Medical Billing Advocates of America consistently finds errors in 50-80% of medical bills, most going undisputed. Common errors: out-of-network charges that should be in-network (per the No Surprises Act of 2022, surprise out-of-network billing in emergencies and at in-network facilities is illegal), duplicate charges (same procedure billed twice), upcoding (billed a higher-tier code than the service merited), services you didn't receive, prescription drugs charged that the hospital pharmacy actually waived. Cash-pay negotiation: hospitals routinely accept 30-50% off list prices from uninsured / self-pay patients (this is how their 'charity care' and 'financial-hardship' programs operate). For insured-but-disputing scenarios: call the EOB's billing dispute line, not the provider's billing department, and the dispute auto-pauses collections for 30+ days.
shortcut: Three-step routine on every medical bill over ~$200: (1) **Compare bill to EOB** — bill amount should match the EOB's patient-responsibility line. If it doesn't, dispute. (2) **Itemize** — request a fully itemized bill (not the summary). Errors hide in the CPT codes. (3) **Negotiate** — uninsured or self-pay? Ask for 30-50% off list. Insured but the EOB shows a billing error? Call the insurer's billing-dispute number; the No Surprises Act (2022) prevents out-of-network charges in emergencies and at in-network facilities. Never pay a medical bill on receipt — there's no benefit to paying on day 1 and the 30-day audit pays for itself many times over.
example:
Maya gets an ER visit. A month later, two documents:

**Provider bill (Mercy ER):**
  Total charges: $8,400
  Insurance paid: $5,200
  Amount owed: **$3,200**
  Due in 30 days.

**Insurance EOB (Aetna):**
  Total billed: $8,400
  Adjusted off (network rate): $1,800
  Insurance paid: $5,200
  **Patient responsibility: $1,400**
  (Deductible $1,000 already met; coinsurance 20% on remaining = $400)

Gap: provider says $3,200, EOB says $1,400. The provider is over-billing by $1,800 — they didn't apply the in-network adjustment.

Maya's action: call Aetna's billing dispute line, reference the EOB. Aetna confirms the network rate. Provider re-bills for $1,400. **Maya saves $1,800 with one phone call.**

Uninsured negotiation example:
Hospital list price for the same visit: $8,400. Self-pay (no insurance) patient calls billing office:
  'I'm self-pay. What's the cash-pay rate?'
  Hospital offers $4,800 (43% off list).
  Counter: 'I can pay $3,500 today via Zelle.'
  Final: $3,500 settled in full.

Key rule: list prices in US healthcare are essentially fiction. The EOB-negotiated rate is the floor; the cash-pay rate sits 30-50% off list. Either path beats paying the bill as printed.
realWorldHint: Use this when a medical bill arrives and you're not sure what you really owe.

title: Monthly payment vs total cost
concept: Dealers love to talk monthly payments because they sound affordable. But total cost = monthly payment × number of months. A $450/month payment over 72 months means you're paying $32,400 total. Always calculate the full cost before signing.
shortcut: Total cost = payment × months. Interest paid = total cost − loan amount. A $25,000 car at $450/month for 72 months costs $32,400 — that's $7,400 in interest.
example:
Loan: $25,000
Payment: $450/month × 72 months
Total: $32,400
Interest: $7,400
realWorldHint: Use this at the dealership when they steer you toward the monthly payment.

title: The hidden cost of '24 more months'
concept: Salespeople love long loan terms because they lower the monthly payment — and increase total interest. Extending from 48 to 72 months can drop your payment $130/month but add $3,800+ in total cost. Focus on the delta between terms, not the headline payment.
shortcut: Total cost difference = (payment_longer × months_longer) − (payment_shorter × months_shorter). Lower payment ≠ better deal. The extra months are pure interest extraction.
example:
Same $25,000 loan:
48 months × $550 = $26,400
72 months × $420 = $30,240
Extra cost of longer term: $3,840

Monthly 'savings' from 48→72: $130
Total cost increase: $3,840
The trade-off is bad.
realWorldHint: Use this before you stretch a car loan to shrink the payment.

title: Down payment math
concept: A down payment doesn't just reduce what you borrow — it eliminates interest on that money. On a 5-year loan at 7%, a $5k down payment saves $5k principal + ~$900 interest = $5,900 in total cost. But there's an opportunity cost: that $5k could've been invested. The math: if your loan rate (after tax) is HIGHER than your expected investment return, down payment wins. At 7% car loan vs 8% stock returns, it's almost a wash — invest if you have other high-rate debt, down-payment if you don't.
shortcut: Down payment = price × down%. Loan = price − down. Interest saved by larger down ≈ extra down × loan rate × term/2. But: opportunity cost. $5k invested at 8% becomes ~$7,300 in 5 years. If your loan rate > expected investment return, down-pay. Otherwise consider investing the extra cash instead.
example:
$30,000 car, 7% APR, 60 months:
0% down: $5,700 interest
20% down ($6,000): borrow $24k, $4,560 interest
Difference: $1,140 interest saved

Opportunity cost check:
$6,000 invested at 8% × 5 yrs ≈ $8,800 (gain $2,800)
Down payment saves $1,140; investing earns $2,800.
If you have no other high-rate debt, the math favors investing the $6k and taking the smaller down.
realWorldHint: Run this before you decide how much to put down on a car.

title: The 20/4/10 rule
concept: Financial experts recommend: 20% down payment, 4-year (48-month) max loan term, and total car costs under 10% of gross monthly income. This rule keeps you from being 'car poor' — spending so much on your car that it squeezes everything else.
shortcut: Max car cost (10% rule) = monthly gross income × 10%. That includes payment + insurance + gas. If you earn $5,000/month gross, max total car costs = $500/month.
example:
Monthly income: $5,000
10% max car cost: $500/month
Includes: payment + insurance + gas
If insurance + gas = $200
Max payment: $300/month
realWorldHint: Use this to know how much car you can actually afford.

title: Car depreciation math
concept: New cars lose about 20% of their value in the first year and roughly 15% per year after that. A $35,000 car is worth about $28,000 after year one. Understanding depreciation helps you decide between new, certified pre-owned, and used.
shortcut: Value after year 1 = price × 80%. Value after year 2 ≈ year 1 value × 85%. Quick estimate: a car loses about half its value in 3-4 years.
example:
New car: $35,000
After year 1 (−20%): $28,000
After year 2 (−15%): $23,800
Lost $11,200 in 2 years
realWorldHint: Use this before buying new to see how fast the value drops.

title: What your car really costs per month
concept: Monthly car cost ≠ monthly payment. The real number includes payment + insurance + gas + maintenance + depreciation. For most cars, that's $300-$400/month ON TOP of the payment. A $400 payment becomes a $700-$800/month total cost.
shortcut: Add payment + ~$150 insurance + ~$150 gas + ~$80 maintenance as baseline non-payment costs. Total monthly ownership = payment + $380 (typical). Add depreciation if you're tracking true cost.
example:
Payment: $400
Insurance: $150
Gas: $200
Maintenance: $80
Total monthly cost: $830

Reality: $830 × 12 = $9,960/year of car expenses, not $4,800.
realWorldHint: Use this to see what a car really costs beyond the payment.

title: Lease vs buy — the 3-year math
concept: The headline lease-vs-buy math ('lease cost vs net buy cost') is a useful first cut, but real lease economics include several fees most quick comparisons skip. A complete lease cost includes: (1) monthly payment × term, (2) acquisition fee (a.k.a. bank fee, typically $595-$995 upfront), (3) disposition fee (charged at lease-end, typically $300-$500 unless you buy out or roll into a new lease with the same captive), (4) sales tax — most states tax the MONTHLY payment, not the full vehicle price, which is a real lease advantage, (5) excess-mileage penalty if you exceed the contracted limit (typical 10K/12K/15K mile/year tiers; overage runs $0.15-$0.30 per mile, per major captive published rates), (6) excess wear-and-tear charges at turn-in. A complete buy cost includes purchase price + sales tax + interest paid − resale value. The honest comparison is: total all-in lease cost vs (total buy cost − end-of-term resale value), over the same horizon. Buying almost always wins if you keep the car 5+ years; leasing can win for high-mileage avoiders who upgrade every 3 years.
shortcut: Full lease cost = (monthly × months) + acquisition fee + disposition fee + (overage miles × overage rate) + tax on monthly. Full buy net cost over same period = (monthly × months) + purchase tax − resale value. Compare totals. Most-overlooked lease cost: the acquisition fee ($595-$995, charged at signing) plus the disposition fee ($300-$500, charged at lease-end). On a 36-month lease that adds $25-$40/month in 'invisible' cost that the headline payment doesn't show.
example:
Realistic 36-month lease vs 36-months-of-ownership compare.

Lease (Honda Civic LX, 12K mi/yr, 36 mo):
  Monthly payment: $350
  × 36 months = $12,600
  Acquisition fee at signing: $695
  Disposition fee at turn-in: $395
  Sales tax on monthly (~8% on $350 × 36) ≈ already in payment, depends on state
  Total all-in lease cost: ~$13,690

Buy (same Civic, 60-mo loan, sell at 36 months):
  Monthly payment: $500
  × 36 months = $18,000 paid
  Estimated resale value at 36 months: ~$20,000
  Net cost: $18,000 − $20,000 = −$2,000 (built $2,000 in equity)

Buying wins by ~$15,690 over the 3-year window.

Lease wins only when:
  - You consistently drive UNDER the mileage allowance (lease return without overage)
  - You'd otherwise sell after 3 years (don't capture the 4-10 year value)
  - You want the latest tech / safety features every 3 years
  - Your state taxes lease monthly payments significantly less than purchase price

One overlooked tax wrinkle: 36 states tax leases on the monthly payment only, not the full vehicle price — that's a real lease advantage for residents of those states. In TX / NY / OH / MN / IL, the full purchase price is taxed upfront on a lease, which erases most of the lease advantage.
realWorldHint: Use this when you're deciding whether to lease or buy.

title: Is the dealer trade-in rip-off worth it?
concept: Dealers offer convenience but lowball trade-in prices. The spread between trade-in and private sale is typically $2,000-$4,000. Private selling takes time (2-4 weeks of effort) but the difference often comes out to $100-$200/hour of effort. Tax wrinkle: in most states, trading in reduces your sales tax base on the new car.
shortcut: Trade-in premium = private sale price − trade-in offer. Effective hourly = premium ÷ estimated hours of selling effort. Tax benefit of trade-in = (trade-in value) × your state sales tax rate.
example:
Car: $11,000 private market, $8,000 trade-in offer
Premium: $3,000
Estimated hours: 20 (photos, listings, calls, test drives, paperwork)
Effective: $150/hour

Tax benefit (trade-in): $8,000 × 8% = $640 less sales tax
Adjusted premium: $3,000 − $640 = $2,360
realWorldHint: Run this before you accept a dealer's trade-in offer.

title: Dealer tactics — what to watch for
concept: Car dealerships have refined their tactics over decades. The 'four-square' worksheet that combines trade-in, down payment, monthly payment, and price into one confusing grid (designed to hide markup). The 'what payment can you afford?' trap (extends the term to inflate your total cost). The F&I (Finance & Insurance) office where they pitch GAP insurance, paint protection, and extended warranties at markup. Financing markup (dealers add 1-3% to the rate the lender quoted them). Document fees (often $300-$700, sometimes negotiable).
shortcut: Negotiate ONE number: out-the-door price. Refuse to discuss monthly payment or trade-in until OTD is locked. Get pre-approved financing from your bank BEFORE walking in. Decline everything in the F&I office (extended warranty, GAP, paint protection) — you can buy these elsewhere for half the price.
example:
The 'monthly payment' trap:
$30,000 car at $500/mo for 60 months = $30,000 paid (0% interest example, ignore)
But $30,000 car at $500/mo for 72 months = $36,000 paid
Same monthly comfort, $6,000 more paid

Dealer F&I markup example:
Lender quotes 6% APR to dealer
Dealer offers you 7.5%
On $25k loan over 5 years: $1,000+ in extra interest, paid as F&I commission
realWorldHint: Keep this in mind the moment you walk onto the lot.

title: Manufacturer vs extended warranty
concept: Most new cars come with a manufacturer warranty: typically 3 years / 36,000 miles bumper-to-bumper, 5 years / 60,000 miles powertrain (varies by automaker — Hyundai/Kia and Mitsubishi offer 10-year powertrain). Extended warranties / service contracts (sold by the dealer F&I office) add 1-7 years for $1,000-$3,000. Consumer Reports surveys of car owners consistently find the majority never use their extended warranty, and those who do recoup less than what they paid on average (per Consumer Reports auto reliability surveys). The expected value is negative — it's insurance against repair anxiety, not a financial product.
shortcut: Default to passing on extended warranties — self-insure instead; consider them only for first-year EVs or repair-expensive European luxury brands.
example:
Extended warranty math:
Cost: $2,000 for 5 extra years
Avg payout (per CR surveys): well under $2k for most buyers
Expected loss: typically several hundred dollars

Alternative: self-insure
Save $33/month → $2,000 by year 5
If no major repair: you keep $2,000
If major repair ($1,500): still net positive $500
realWorldHint: Use this when the finance office pitches an extended warranty.

title: Student loan monthly payment
concept: Standard 10-year repayment costs about $100-$120 per $10,000 borrowed at typical 4-7% rates. A $30k loan ≈ $300-$360/month. A $50k loan ≈ $500-$600/month. This rule is accurate within 10% of the actual amortized payment.
shortcut: Per $10k borrowed at 4-7% APR over 10 years: ~$100-$120/month. Higher rate = closer to $120. Quick mental math: divide your balance by $10k, multiply by your per-$10k rate.
example:
Loan $40,000:
$40k ÷ $10k = 4
× $110 (~5% APR) = $440/month

Loan $25,000 at 6%:
2.5 × $115 = ~$287/month
Actual amortized: $278 (within $10)
realWorldHint: Use this to estimate your monthly payment before repayment starts.

title: Total cost of student loans
concept: Total repayment = monthly payment × number of months. Subtract the original loan to find total interest. A 10-year loan at 5-6% typically costs ~25-30% of original balance in interest. $40k loan? Expect $10k-$12k extra in interest.
shortcut: Total cost = payment × months. Interest = total − loan. Interest as % = interest ÷ loan × 100. Quick benchmark: 10-yr loan at 5-6% = ~28% interest premium.
example:
$30,000 loan, $318/mo × 120 months:
Total: $38,160
Interest: $8,160
Interest %: 27.2%

Within the 25-30% benchmark for standard repayment.
realWorldHint: Use this to see what your loans really cost over their full life.

title: Refinancing savings
concept: Refinancing replaces your current loan with a new one at a lower interest rate. The savings come from the rate difference applied to your balance. Dropping from 6% to 4% on a $40,000 balance saves roughly $800/year in interest.
shortcut: Annual interest saving ≈ balance × (old rate − new rate). $40,000 × (6% − 4%) = $800/year. Over 10 years, that's $8,000 in savings — but you lose federal loan protections.
example:
Balance: $40,000
Old rate: 6%, New rate: 4%
Annual saving: $40,000 × 2% = $800
10-year saving: ~$8,000
realWorldHint: Run this before refinancing to weigh savings against lost protections.

title: Income-driven repayment
concept: ⚠️ **This lesson covers a topic with unusually volatile rules.** Income-driven repayment plans have been in active flux since the 2024 federal court rulings vacating parts of SAVE. The Department of Education has issued repeated transitional guidance through 2025-26 directing affected borrowers between plans. **Before making any IDR decision, always check the current state at studentaid.gov and run your numbers through the official FSA Loan Simulator — not this lesson alone.** With that caveat: IDR caps federal student-loan payments at a percentage of your 'discretionary income' (income above a poverty-line multiplier, per Federal Student Aid). The legacy plans — PAYE, IBR (original and new), ICR — use different formulas (10-20% of discretionary), different poverty-line multipliers (100% or 150%), different family-size adjustments, and different forgiveness timelines (20 years for some, 25 for others). SAVE was the most generous and is now permanently closed. The big 2026 change: OBBBA created the **Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP)** — the default income-driven option for borrowers whose FIRST loans are disbursed on/after July 1, 2026 (payments scale 1%-10% of income with a $10/mo floor, forgiveness after 30 years). Borrowers with older loans are being migrated into IBR, which remains the most stable plan because it's statutory rather than regulatory. Only federal Direct Loans qualify for IDR/RAP; private loans don't.
shortcut: Any mental estimate is rough — your real IDR payment depends on plan, family size, and filing. Quote the FSA Loan Simulator at studentaid.gov, never a number you did in your head.
example:
Baseline illustration ONLY (canonical IBR-style 10%/150% formula):

Income: $50,000, single, no dependents
Federal poverty line (1 person, 2026, per HHS): $15,960
Poverty line × 1.5: $23,940
Discretionary income: $50,000 − $23,940 = $26,060
Monthly ≈ $26,060 × 10% ÷ 12 ≈ $217

Real-world reality check:
— Old PAYE: 10% of discretionary, 150% poverty multiplier, 20-yr forgiveness. Closing to new enrollees.
— New IBR: 10% of discretionary, 150% poverty, 20-yr forgiveness for new borrowers from 2014+ (10/20 plan).
— Old IBR: 15% of discretionary, 150% poverty, 25-yr forgiveness.
— ICR: 20% of discretionary, 100% poverty. Highest payment, lowest income protection.
— SAVE: closed permanently; borrowers migrated into IBR or RAP.
— RAP (OBBBA, for first loans disbursed on/after July 1, 2026): payment scales 1%-10% of total AGI by income band, $10/mo floor, forgiveness after 30 years.

The gap between IBR (10% on 150%) and ICR (20% on 100%) on the same $50K income can be ~$200/month. That's why running the simulator beats running the mental math here.
realWorldHint: Use this if your federal loan payment feels unaffordable on your income.

title: PSLF forgiveness math
concept: Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF) forgives remaining federal loan balance after 120 qualifying payments (10 years) while working for a qualifying employer. ⚠️ A March 2025 executive order narrowed the definition of a 'qualifying employer' (excluding organizations engaged in certain activities); the rule is in active litigation, so confirm your employer still qualifies at studentaid.gov before relying on PSLF. The key math: total paid = IDR payment × 120 months. Forgiven amount = original balance + accrued interest − total paid.
shortcut: PSLF total paid = monthly IDR payment × 120. Forgiveness amount = remaining balance at month 120. If you pay $250/month for 10 years = $30,000 paid. If balance started at $80,000, you could get $50,000+ forgiven.
example:
Loan: $80,000
IDR payment: $250/month
10 years = $30,000 paid
Forgiven: $50,000+
(balance grew with interest)
realWorldHint: Use this if you work in public service and might qualify for forgiveness.

title: Does your employer pay your student loans?
concept: If your employer offers it, IRC § 127 lets them contribute up to $5,250/year tax-free toward your student loans — made permanent under the OBBBA in 2025. Adoption is still uncommon: around 26% of employers offered it in 2024 (per SHRM 2024 Employee Benefits Survey), heavily skewed toward larger employers, professional services, healthcare, and tech. So this isn't a default benefit to assume — but if your benefits package includes it, it's effectively a $437.50/month tax-free raise that goes straight to principal.
shortcut: Annual benefit ÷ 12 = monthly principal contribution. Multi-year value: benefit × years + interest you avoid (rough: benefit × your rate × half the remaining years, because the principal shrinks linearly). Check your benefits portal for 'student loan repayment' or 'education assistance' line items — it's often filed under the wrong header.
example:
Your employer offers the max $5,250/yr (per IRC § 127):
Monthly: $437.50 straight to principal

5 years of full benefit:
$26,250 paid by employer
+ ~$2,000 in interest you avoid (on a 6% loan)
Total value: ~$28,250 — equivalent to a $5,650/yr tax-free raise.
realWorldHint: Check this in case your employer quietly offers loan-repayment help.

title: Your loans are growing while you wait
concept: Unsubsidized federal loans accrue interest from disbursement. The 6-month grace period after graduation doesn't pause interest — it keeps piling up and is added to what you owe. (A 2023 federal rule means this accrued interest is no longer automatically capitalized — folded into principal — when you enter repayment, but you still owe every dollar of it, and it can capitalize later at triggers like leaving an income-driven plan or default.) A $25,000 loan at 6.5% accrues ~$800 during grace alone. Most new grads don't realize this.
shortcut: Daily interest = balance × rate ÷ 365. Grace period total = daily × 180 days. Paying that interest during grace keeps it from being added to your balance (and from capitalizing later), saving money long-term.
example:
$25,000 unsubsidized at 6.5%:
Daily interest: $4.45
Grace period (180 days): $801
New balance at repayment start: $25,801

Interest-only during grace ($135/mo):
Balance stays $25,000 → save $801 + future interest on it
realWorldHint: Use this during your 6-month grace period before interest piles up.

title: Parent PLUS vs private — which costs less?
concept: Parent PLUS loans carry a 9.07% fixed rate (2026-27 academic year) + a 4.228% origination fee deducted upfront. Private parent loans start as low as 5.09% with no origination. For a parent with good credit, private can save $10k+ over 10 years on a $30k loan. But PLUS offers federal protections (IDR, deferment, PSLF) that private doesn't. Note: OBBBA caps new Parent PLUS borrowing at $20,000/year per student and $65,000 lifetime per student for loans first disbursed on/after July 1, 2026. Rates reset annually each July based on the May Treasury auction.
shortcut: Annual interest difference = balance × (PLUS rate − private rate). Over 10 years × 10. Origination fee adds to PLUS cost upfront. Trade-off: ~$10k savings on private vs federal protections.
example:
$30,000 borrowed:
PLUS at 9.07%: ~$2,721/yr interest + $1,268 origination upfront
Private at 5.5%: ~$1,650/yr interest, no fee

Annual diff: ~$1,071
10-year diff: ~$10,710 + $1,268 = $11,978 saved with private
realWorldHint: Use this when financing a kid's education and weighing federal vs private.

title: Subsidized vs unsubsidized loans
concept: Subsidized loans are need-based and capped — undergrads with demonstrated financial need on their FAFSA may qualify, up to annual limits ($3,500-$5,500/year per Federal Student Aid). On a subsidized loan, the government pays the interest while you're in school, during the 6-month grace period, and during qualified deferment. Unsubsidized loans are available to all eligible students but accrue interest from disbursement onward. Most graduate loans and Parent PLUS are unsubsidized. The difference compounds: a $25k subsidized loan stays at $25k through graduation; a $25k unsubsidized loan grows to ~$28k over four years at 5.5%.
shortcut: Borrow in this order: subsidized first (the government covers the interest in school), then unsubsidized, then Parent PLUS, then private last.
example:
$25,000 borrowed, 4 years in school + 6 months grace, 5.5% interest:
Subsidized: balance at repayment start = $25,000
Unsubsidized: balance at repayment start ≈ $31,000

Difference: ~$6,000 in accrued interest you also owe. Pay it during school and grace so it can't capitalize later (for example, if you leave an income-driven plan) — that is what avoids paying ~$5,000 more in lifetime interest on it.
realWorldHint: Use this when you're accepting financial aid and choosing what to borrow.

title: Federal loan protections you lose by refinancing
concept: Refinance salespeople pitch lower rates without mentioning what you give up. Refinancing federal loans to private permanently forfeits: IDR plans (payment based on income), PSLF (forgiveness after 10 years in public service — though a March 2025 executive order narrowed which employers qualify, now in litigation), federal forbearance (pause payments during hardship), death/disability discharge (federal loans wiped if you die or become totally disabled), and any future federal relief (like the COVID-era pause). You CANNOT refi back to federal once you've gone private — it's a one-way door.
shortcut: Refinancing federal loans is a one-way door: you lose IDR, PSLF, and hardship pauses for good. Refi only if you'll never need them and save 2%+. For public-service workers, almost never.
example:
Refi tradeoff example:
Federal loan: $40k at 6%, 10-year repayment, $444/mo
Private refi: $40k at 4.5%, 10-year repayment, $415/mo
Savings: $29/month = $3,480 over 10 years

What you give up:
— PSLF (could be $20k-$80k forgiven if you'd qualify)
— IDR (payments could drop dramatically if you lose your job)
— COVID-era pause (saved typical borrower $5k-$10k)
Verdict: only worth it if you're confident none of those protections matter for you.
realWorldHint: Read this before a refinance salesperson pitches you a lower rate.

title: Spot the imposter scam
concept: The most-reported fraud in America is the imposter scam: someone pretending to be your bank, the government, or a company you trust. The play is always the same three beats — (1) manufactured urgency ('your account is compromised'), (2) borrowed authority (caller ID can be spoofed to show your bank's real name and number), (3) an unusual action only a scammer would request: move your money to a 'safe account,' Zelle it to yourself, read back a security code, or buy gift cards. Per the FTC, your bank will never call or text you asking you to transfer money or share a passcode — and fake bank fraud-alert texts were among the most-reported text scams (FTC, 2024 data).
shortcut: One rule beats every script: hang up and call the number on the back of your card. Real fraud departments never mind a callback — only imposters need you to stay on the line. Urgency + secrecy + 'move your money' = imposter, every time.
example:
Text: 'FRAUD ALERT: Did you authorize $480 at Walmart? Reply NO.'
You reply — your phone rings. 'Bank security' says move your checking to a 'safe account' now.

The tells:
— Real banks freeze fraud internally; they never need YOU to move money
— Caller ID showing the bank's number proves nothing (spoofable)
— The callback test costs 60 seconds and defeats 100% of imposters
realWorldHint: Use this the moment any call or text about your money creates urgency.

title: Payment methods scammers love
concept: Every scam funnels to the same question: HOW do they want the money? Payment methods differ wildly in reversibility. Credit cards carry the strongest federal dispute rights; debit cards have protections but the cash leaves your account first. P2P apps (Zelle, Venmo, Cash App) treat a payment YOU sent as authorized — recovery is rare even when you were tricked. Wire transfers, gift cards, and crypto-ATM deposits are effectively cash: gone in minutes. That's why the FTC's rule of thumb is absolute: anyone who DEMANDS payment by gift card, wire, or crypto is running a scam — no legitimate business or government agency does that.
shortcut: Reversibility ladder, top to bottom: credit card → debit card → P2P apps → wire / gift cards / crypto. The harder a payment is to reverse, the harder a scammer pushes it. The method IS the tell: when someone else picks the payment and it sits low on the ladder, walk away.
example:
Same $500 'purchase', four endings:
Credit card → dispute it, provisional credit, federal billing rights
Debit card → bank investigates; your cash is missing meanwhile
Zelle to a stranger → treated as authorized; usually gone
Gift card codes read over the phone → cashed out in minutes, gone

'Pay only by gift card / wire / crypto ATM' = scam, 100% of the time (FTC)
realWorldHint: Check the payment method before you check anything else about a deal.

title: Your credit file: free reports, disputes, freezes
concept: Three federal rights most people never use. (1) Free reports: you can pull your credit report from EACH of the three bureaus free every week at AnnualCreditReport.com — the only federally authorized source (made permanent in 2023, per FTC). (2) Free disputes: if a report has an error, the bureau must investigate, generally within 30 days, at no cost (FCRA). Errors are common enough that checking matters. (3) Free freezes: a security freeze blocks new-account openings in your name; federal law (2018) made placing and lifting freezes free at all three bureaus. A freeze doesn't touch your score, your existing cards, or your ability to use credit — it only blocks NEW accounts until you thaw it.
shortcut: Three free moves: PULL (AnnualCreditReport.com, weekly, each bureau), DISPUTE (in writing; bureau must answer in ~30 days), FREEZE (all three bureaus, free, zero score effect). If you're not opening credit soon, the freeze is the cheapest identity-theft defense that exists.
example:
Data breach in the news:
1. Freeze at Equifax + Experian + TransUnion — ~15 min total, $0
2. Pull all three reports — $0
3. Spot an account you don't recognize → dispute in writing — $0

Applying for a card next month? Thaw the freeze for a window — also $0.
Total cost of the full defense: $0. (FTC / CFPB)
realWorldHint: Use this after any data-breach headline — the whole defense costs $0.

title: Negotiate the offer — math and script
concept: Negotiation is a 10-minute conversation that repeats its payoff every year of your career. Three mechanics: (1) Anchoring — the first number spoken frames everything after it, so when asked for your expectations, ask for THEIR budgeted range first: 'What range did you have budgeted for the role?' (2) The counter — recruiters budget for counters; a respectful, data-backed counter does not get offers pulled: 'Based on the role and market data, I was expecting closer to $X — is there flexibility?' Counter on the whole package (base, signing bonus, equity, start date, PTO), not just base. (3) Compounding — a higher base repeats every year, and every future percentage raise and next-job offer builds on it. A $3,000 win at 28 is tens of thousands by 40 before investing a cent of it.
shortcut: Your raise is just salary × the %. The real prize is compounding: a higher base lifts every future raise and your next offer, so a small win now is tens of thousands by 40.
example:
Offer: $70,000. You counter at $74,900 (+7%) with market data.
They settle at $73,000 → +$3,000/year.

10-year floor: $30,000 extra (before raises compound it)
Every future % raise now builds on $73k, not $70k.
Time invested: one slightly awkward 10-minute call.
realWorldHint: Use this the day an offer letter lands — before you reply.

title: Your 401(k) when you leave a job
concept: Leaving a job hands you four options for your 401(k): leave it, roll it to the new employer's plan, roll it to an IRA, or cash out. Cashing out is the expensive trap — income tax plus a 10% penalty under age 59½ (per IRS) — yet roughly 41% of departing employees do it (UBC Sauder/HBR study of 162,000 separations). The subtler trap is HOW you roll: a DIRECT rollover moves money custodian-to-custodian, untouched. An INDIRECT rollover (they mail YOU a check) triggers mandatory 20% withholding (per IRS) — and you must deposit the FULL original amount within 60 days, replacing the withheld 20% from your own pocket, or the gap is taxed and penalized as a distribution.
