shortcut: Say the magic words: 'direct rollover.' Cash-out cost ≈ balance × (your tax rate + 10%) under 59½. Indirect-rollover trap: the check arrives 20% light, and the 60-day clock expects you to top it back up.
example:
$20,000 balance, 22% bracket, age 30:

Cash out → lose ~$6,400 (22% + 10% = 32%), keep ~$13,600
Indirect rollover → check = $16,000; must deposit $20,000 within 60 days (find $4,000 yourself)
Direct rollover → $20,000 moves whole. Costs $0.

(IRS rollover rules; Topic 413)
realWorldHint: Use this in your last two weeks at any job — before HR mails a check.

title: Health coverage when you leave a job
concept: Losing job-based insurance opens two paths and one clock. COBRA lets you keep your exact plan (same doctors, same deductible progress) for up to 18 months — but you pay the FULL premium plus up to a 2% admin fee (102% of plan cost, per DOL), because the employer subsidy is what vanished. The marketplace path: losing job coverage triggers a Special Enrollment Period — 60 days to enroll at HealthCare.gov, where income-based subsidies (calculated on your NEW, lower income) often beat COBRA by hundreds a month. The clock: 60 days to elect COBRA too (from the later of the election notice or coverage ending). And one powerful wrinkle: COBRA is RETROACTIVE to your coverage-loss date if you elect within the window.
shortcut: Compare two numbers before paying anything: COBRA ≈ full plan premium × 1.02 vs. a marketplace quote at your new income. Both decisions get ~60 days. The backstop play: you can hold off electing COBRA and elect retroactively within the window only if something happens — but calendar the deadline.
example:
Employer plan total cost: $650/mo (you paid $150, employer $500):

COBRA: $650 × 1.02 = $663/mo — sticker shock is the norm
Marketplace, subsidized at reduced income: ~$280/mo
Difference: $383/mo ≈ $4,600/yr

Same 60-day window for both paths. (DOL COBRA guide; HealthCare.gov)
realWorldHint: Use this the week a job ends — before the COBRA letter scares you into overpaying.

title: Payday loans, cash advances & overdrafts — the real APR
concept: A payday loan's fee sounds small: '$15 per $100 for two weeks' is the common structure ($10–$30 per $100 depending on state, per CFPB). Annualized, that's roughly 400% APR — against ~22% on even an expensive credit card. The trap is the rollover: if you can't repay in 14 days, you pay another fee to extend, and the CFPB found most borrowers end up re-borrowing rather than repaying — fees can pass the original loan within months. Cash-advance apps often repackage similar economics as 'tips' and 'express fees.' Overdrafts are the same lesson in miniature: a $35 fee to cover a $20 shortfall for three days is an astronomical effective rate — though fees now vary wildly by bank (several large banks charge $0–$10), and a polite call often gets a first fee waived.
shortcut: APR ≈ (fee per $100 ÷ 100) × (365 ÷ term days) × 100. So $15 per $100 for 14 days ≈ 391%. Overdraft check: fee ÷ amount covered × 100 = the instant percentage. Waiver script: 'Hi — I've banked with you for X years and overdrew by accident this week. Could you waive the fee as a courtesy?'
example:
Borrow $300 for 2 weeks at $15 per $100:
Fee: $45 → repay $345
APR: (15 ÷ 100) × (365 ÷ 14) ≈ 391%
Roll it over 4 times: $180 in fees on a $300 loan — 60% in two months, principal still owed.

Overdraft: $35 fee covering a $20 shortfall = 175% of the amount, instantly.
(CFPB payday-loan cost data)
realWorldHint: Use this before any 'quick cash' decision — the APR math takes ten seconds.

title: Upside down: negative equity on a car loan
concept: You're 'upside down' when you owe more than the car is worth — and it's now mainstream: in Q1 2026, 30.9% of trade-ins toward new cars carried negative equity, averaging $7,183 owed beyond the car's value (Edmunds). The drivers: long loan terms (72–84 months) pay principal slower than cars depreciate. The most misleading phrase on the lot is 'we'll pay off your loan no matter what you owe' — they don't pay it off, they ROLL the shortfall into your NEW loan, so you drive off underwater on the new car from day one. On-time payments don't prevent any of this; depreciation simply outruns amortization on long loans. Escape routes, best to worst: keep the car and keep paying (equity returns as the loan amortizes), pay the gap in cash if you must trade, or at absolute minimum walk in knowing your number before the dealer frames it.
shortcut: Equity = car's value − loan payoff. Negative = upside down by that much. Before any trade-in: look up the car's market value, call the lender for the exact payoff, subtract. Judge every dealer offer with that shortfall ADDED to the new loan.
example:
Car's market value: $14,000. Loan payoff: $19,500.
Equity: 14,000 − 19,500 = −$5,500 (upside down)

Dealer 'pays off your loan' on a $30,000 new car:
New loan = $30,000 + $5,500 = $35,500
— underwater on the new car before leaving the lot.

(Edmunds Q1 2026: 30.9% of trade-ins, avg −$7,183)
realWorldHint: Run the equity math before any dealership visit — know your number before they do.

title: Shrinkflation — same price, smaller box
concept: When a price can't rise invisibly, the package shrinks instead. The GAO found downsized grocery products carried average unit-price increases of 12% (paper towels) to 32% (coffee) across 2019–2024 — while the shelf price looked unchanged (GAO-25-107451). It's legal, and it works precisely because shoppers track prices, not quantities; research shows people respond far less to downsizing than to an equivalent price hike. The defense is one number: the unit price — price ÷ quantity, in $/oz, per-sheet, or per-load. It's printed in small type on most shelf tags (a dozen-plus states require it), and it's the only number shrinkflation can't fool.
shortcut: Unit price = total price ÷ quantity. Shrink % = (old size ÷ new size − 1) × 100 — a 16 oz → 14 oz 'same-price' shrink is 16/14 − 1 ≈ +14% per ounce. Compare $/oz across brands AND across time; ignore the sticker.
example:
Cereal: $4.99 for 18 oz → $4.99 for 15.3 oz
Old unit price: 27.7¢/oz
New unit price: 32.6¢/oz
Effective increase: 18 ÷ 15.3 − 1 ≈ +17.6% per oz — at the 'same' price.

(GAO: downsized categories averaged 12–32% unit-price hikes)
realWorldHint: Use the unit-price line on the shelf tag — it's the one number the package can't shrink.

title: How filing actually works
concept: Filing a return is a reconciliation, not a bill. Your employer withholds estimated tax from every paycheck all year (set by your W-4); the return computes what you actually owed. A refund means you overpaid through withholding - it's your own money coming back, not a bonus. The pipeline: your W-2 must be sent by the end of January (IRS); you file by April 15; e-file with direct deposit and most refunds arrive within ~21 days (IRS). Free ways to file: IRS Free File guided software if your AGI is $89,000 or less (2026 season), Free File Fillable Forms at any income, VITA in-person help if you make about $69,000 or less, and MilTax for military families at any income. (IRS Direct File ran 2024-2025 and was discontinued for 2026.)
shortcut: Refund = your own overpaid withholding coming back. The free path: W-2 lands by end of January -> Free File if under $89K AGI -> e-file + direct deposit -> ~21 days.
example:
Single, $52,000 salary, one W-2:
1. W-2 arrives by end of January
2. AGI under $89,000 -> IRS Free File guided software, $0
3. E-file + direct deposit by April 15
4. Refund (if any) in ~21 days

A paid preparer for this return buys convenience, not a bigger refund - the numbers are the numbers. (IRS)
realWorldHint: Pull this up the week your W-2 arrives - the free path takes one evening.

title: Building credit from zero
concept: A FICO score doesn't exist until your file has at least one account open 6+ months AND one account reported to a bureau in the last 6 months (myFICO). Three starter tools: (1) a secured card - your refundable deposit (usually $200 minimum) typically becomes your credit line, and on-time use can graduate it to a regular card with the deposit returned; (2) becoming an authorized user on a trusted person's old card - the account's history can appear on YOUR report (issuer-dependent) and you carry zero legal liability for the debt (CFPB); (3) a credit-builder loan - the money sits locked in savings while your payments get reported (CFPB). What moves the score: payment history is ~35% of FICO and utilization ~30% - so one small recurring charge, autopaid in full, does almost all the work.
shortcut: One small card + one recurring bill + autopay in full. Six months of on-time payments = a score exists. Keep the balance tiny relative to the limit.
example:
22, no credit history:
1. Secured card, $200 deposit -> $200 limit
2. Put one subscription (~$15/mo) on it
3. Autopay the FULL statement every month
4. ~6 months later: a FICO score exists; the card can graduate and the $200 comes back

Late payments get reported the same way on-time ones do - autopay is the whole game. (myFICO / CFPB)
realWorldHint: Setting up a first card? Put ONE small subscription on it and turn on full-balance autopay before you leave the app.

title: Disputing a charge: your rights
concept: Two different rulebooks. CREDIT cards (Fair Credit Billing Act): you have 60 days from the date of the statement containing the error to dispute in writing, and your maximum liability for unauthorized use is $50 - and the major card networks contractually take that to $0. DEBIT cards (Regulation E): speed sets your cap - report within 2 business days of learning about it and you're liable for at most $50; report within 60 days of the statement and it's up to $500; wait longer and the losses can be unlimited. For billing mistakes (double charge, wrong amount, item never arrived), contacting the merchant first is usually fastest - but the issuer dispute (chargeback) is your legal backstop, and banks generally provide provisional credit while they investigate.
shortcut: Credit card: 60-day clock from the statement, $50 max on fraud (usually $0). Debit card: speed is everything - 2 days = $50 cap, 60 days = $500, later = no cap. Report fast, in writing.
example:
Unknown $214 charge on your credit card statement:
1. Don't recognize it? Check the merchant name online (many bill under odd names)
2. Still unknown -> dispute with your issuer IN WRITING within 60 days of that statement
3. Issuer investigates; your fraud liability tops out at $50 (networks: $0)

Same charge on a DEBIT card? Report it the day you see it - the $50 cap only holds for 2 business days. (FTC / CFPB)
realWorldHint: See a charge you don't recognize? The clock is already running - check it today, not at the end of the month.

title: Checking accounts: stop paying for your own money
concept: Three checks decide whether your bank quietly costs you money. (1) Overdraft opt-in: under Regulation E, a bank cannot charge overdraft fees on DEBIT-card and ATM transactions unless you explicitly opted in - the default is the purchase is simply declined, free. (Checks and recurring payments aren't covered by that protection.) The fee landscape is now split: many banks charge $0 or $10, while others still charge ~$34 per overdraft. (2) Monthly maintenance fees: about 95% are waivable, usually by direct deposit or a minimum balance - and nearly half of basic checking accounts are free outright (Bankrate 2025). (3) Insurance: confirm FDIC (banks) or NCUA (credit unions) coverage - $250,000 per depositor, per institution, per ownership category.
shortcut: Three questions for any checking account: Am I opted IN to debit overdraft? (Opted out = declined free.) Is my monthly fee waived? (Direct deposit usually does it.) Is it FDIC/NCUA insured? ($250K.)
example:
New job, picking an account:
1. Decline debit overdraft 'coverage' - a declined card costs $0; an overdraft can cost $34
2. Set up direct deposit -> monthly fee waived at most banks
3. Confirm FDIC/NCUA on the bank's site

Paying $12/month in maintenance fees is $144/year for a service that's free across the street. (CFPB / FDIC / Bankrate 2025)
realWorldHint: Opening any account, the teller will offer 'overdraft protection' on your debit card - now you know what that actually means.

title: Renters insurance: the $15/month most people skip
concept: Your landlord's insurance covers the BUILDING - never your stuff. Renters insurance (average ~$171/year, NAIC 2022 - roughly $15/month) covers three things: your possessions (fire, theft, vandalism and other named perils - flood and earthquake excluded), liability if you, your family, or your pet injures someone or damages property, and additional living expenses - the hotel and meals if a covered loss makes your place unlivable. One choice matters at purchase: actual cash value pays what your used stuff was worth (depreciated); replacement cost pays what NEW equivalents cost - for roughly 10% more premium, it's the better protection (III). About 57% of renters carry it, and roughly half of landlords now require it in the lease.
shortcut: Landlord's policy = the building. ~$15/month = your stuff + lawsuits + a hotel if it burns. Pick REPLACEMENT COST, not actual cash value.
example:
Apartment fire next door, smoke ruins your things:
- Landlord's policy: rebuilds the walls. Pays you $0.
- Your renters policy: replaces possessions, covers the 3 weeks in temporary housing

5-year-old laptop stolen:
- Actual cash value: pays its depreciated worth (maybe $200)
- Replacement cost: pays for a comparable NEW one (III / NAIC)
realWorldHint: Signing a lease this year? Quote renters insurance the same day - it's the cheapest line on the move-in list.

title: Auto insurance without overpaying
concept: Average full coverage now runs about $2,700/year (Bankrate, June 2026) - and the spread between insurers for the SAME driver is huge, which makes shopping the biggest lever. State minimums vary wildly (Florida requires no bodily-injury liability at all; California raised its floor to 30/60/15 in 2025) and are rarely enough - the common adequacy guidance is 100/300/100 for real protection (Consumer Reports). Four verified ways to pay less: (1) re-quote every 1-2 years - 'price optimization' (charging loyal non-shoppers more) is a documented industry practice that ~20 states restrict; (2) bundle auto with renters/home (~10-25% off, but compare the final total); (3) raise your deductible IF you can cover it from savings - $500 to $1,000 typically trims roughly 5-15% off the total premium; (4) on an old car, drop collision/comprehensive when that part of the premium exceeds ~10% of the car's value (III's rule of thumb).
shortcut: Re-quote every year or two - loyalty literally costs money. Bundle, raise the deductible you can actually cover, and when comp+collision costs more than 10% of the car's value, drop it.
example:
Renewal letter: up $400 for no reason:
1. Get 3 quotes (same coverage levels) - 30 minutes
2. Ask current insurer to match - they often do for shoppers
3. 12-year-old car worth $3,000 with $480/yr comp+collision? That's 16% of the car's value - drop it and self-insure

The quietest tax on autopilot customers is the loyalty penalty. (III / Consumer Reports / Bankrate 2026)
realWorldHint: When the renewal letter lands, that's the moment - 30 minutes of quotes is the highest-paid half hour of your year.

title: Beneficiaries: 10 minutes that override your will
concept: Accounts with named beneficiaries - 401(k)s, IRAs, life insurance, and payable-on-death (POD) bank accounts - pass directly to whoever is on the FORM, regardless of what your will says. The Supreme Court has enforced this even against an ex-spouse who waived the money in a divorce (Kennedy v. DuPont, 2009): the form controls. Two more rules worth knowing: under ERISA, your spouse is automatically your 401(k) beneficiary unless they sign a notarized waiver (IRAs work differently); and a CONTINGENT beneficiary only inherits if every primary is gone - so name a backup. The whole defense is a 10-minute audit: check the beneficiary on your 401(k), IRA, life insurance, and bank accounts, and re-check after every marriage, divorce, birth, or death (FINRA).
shortcut: The FORM beats the will - every time. Audit four places: 401(k), IRA, life insurance, bank POD. Name a backup. Re-check after every big life event.
example:
Divorced two years ago, never touched the 401(k) form:
- Will says everything to your kids
- Form still names the ex-spouse
-> The ex-spouse gets the 401(k). The Supreme Court has enforced exactly this.

The fix: log in, update the beneficiary, add a contingent. Ten minutes, $0. (DOL / FINRA / Kennedy v. DuPont)
realWorldHint: Next time you log into your 401(k), spend the extra two minutes on the beneficiary tab - it outranks your will.
